problem_statement:
## Description
In the OpenTitan life cycle controller (`lc_ctrl`), a transition to the terminal Scrap state can use the wrong life cycle counter during the second OTP (One-Time Programmable) programming pass. In the reported Return Merchandise Authorization (RMA) to Scrap transition, the controller first issues a counter-programming request for counter value 16, which is the value required for Scrap. During the later state-programming pass, however, the transition logic falls back to the current counter input and requests 8 instead of keeping 16, causing the update to the Scrap state to fail.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the `lc_ctrl_state_transition` block in the life cycle controller IP, which computes the next life cycle state and next life cycle counter for life cycle transitions.

## Expected Behavior
For a valid RMA-to-Scrap transition, once the earlier counter-programming pass has requested counter value 16 for the Scrap transition, the later state-programming pass must continue to request the Scrap state together with counter value 16. The transition must remain valid in that second pass and must not be rejected because the requested counter falls back to 8.

## Actual Behavior
When the finite state machine (FSM) reaches `TransProgSt` for the state-programming pass, the logic recomputes the next counter from the current counter input and requests 8 instead of 16, so the Scrap state programming step fails even though the transition itself is valid.

## Trigger Condition
This bug occurs in the second OTP programming pass of an RMA-to-Scrap transition, specifically when the FSM is in `TransProgSt` and the current counter input seen by the transition logic is 8 after the earlier counter-programming request.

title: [lc_ctrl] Do not assert escalate_en in post transition state
body:
Although the post-transition state is a virtual scrap state, we should not assert `escalate_en` in order to avoid accidental triggering of alerts and escalation sequences. Such escalation sequences typically lead to lead to autonomous system resets, and that could cause issues with the life cycle transition status readout via the life cycle TAP.

Addresses https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/7251

This tracks an offline discussion between Michael and I.

Issue:
When lc transition handshake finished without error, LC_CTRL goes to PostTrans state. 
In lc_ctrl_signal_decode.sv, this will turn on `escalation_en` signal:
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/lc_ctrl/rtl/lc_ctrl_signal_decode.sv#L179

Michael and I found this `escalation_en` will trigger alert, and can potentially trigger `reset` (depends on how alert_handler is configured). We believe this behavior is not ideal because this automatically triggered `reset` might block user from using TAP to access LC_CTRL registers.
We plan to not turn on `escalation_en` when reaches PostTrans state.

Screenshot as below:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11466553/124972887-b908e100-dfdf-11eb-8367-9099d34c0bda.png)

@msfschaffner, please correct me if I misunderstand any part.

Thanks,
Cindy

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan life cycle controller (`lc_ctrl`) enters an internal post-transition FSM state (`PostTransSt`) after a life cycle transition handshake completes successfully. In that state, software or debug logic may need to read the transition result through the life cycle Test Access Port (TAP). The bug is in the `lc_ctrl` output decode path that drives life cycle enable signals while the controller is in `PostTransSt`.

## Expected Behavior
While `lc_ctrl` is in `PostTransSt`, it must remain in a post-transition holding state rather than behaving like an escalation-related state. `lc_escalate_en_o` must stay deasserted, and normal life cycle permission outputs, including `lc_cpu_en_o`, must remain deasserted. A real escalation or scrap-handling state, such as `EscalateSt`, may still assert `lc_escalate_en_o`.

## Actual Behavior
When a transition completes without error and the FSM enters `PostTransSt`, `lc_ctrl` asserts `lc_escalate_en_o`. That assertion can trigger the Alert Handler and, depending on configuration, start an escalation sequence that resets the system. As a result, a successful transition can interfere with reading the transition status through the TAP.

## Affected Function
This affects the `lc_ctrl` IP's post-transition signal decode logic, specifically how `PostTransSt` drives `lc_escalate_en_o` and other life cycle permission outputs.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when a life cycle transition handshake finishes successfully and the `lc_ctrl` FSM moves into `PostTransSt`. In that condition, the design raises the escalation output even though the controller is only holding the successful transition result for readout.

title: [kmac] Latch Entropy Mode when ready
body:
This commit allows the kmac_entropy module to latch the entropy mode
when it is out from `StReset` state. This is related to the issue #6831

In previous design, the SW may change the entropy mode at any time if
the module is not operating. But internal FSM did not expect the sudden
change of the entropy_mode.

It is decided to latch the entropy mode and not affected by the SW
change after the SW setting entropy_ready. To change the mode, SW need
to reset the IP.

It is intentional to not allow FSM to move back to `StReset` as in
`StReset` the entropy module generates garbage entropy to SHA3 core for
ROM_CTRL to verify its image.

problem_statement:
## Description
The KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) IP's `kmac_entropy` submodule does not keep the selected entropy source stable after software finishes configuration. Once software asserts `entropy_ready` and the block has already completed an initial entropy-seeding cycle, a later write to the `CFG.entropy_mode` register can still affect the live entropy path even though the IP has not been reset.

## Expected Behavior
After `entropy_ready` is asserted, the entropy mode for the current KMAC session must remain fixed until the KMAC IP is reset and configured again. A software write to `CFG.entropy_mode` after that point must not change how a later entropy refresh is handled. For example, if the session was configured to use EDN (Entropy Distribution Network) entropy, a subsequent refresh in the same session should still request and consume EDN-provided seed data, even if software writes `EntropyModeNone` before the refresh.

## Actual Behavior
After a previous operation has completed and the entropy block is back in its ready state, `kmac_entropy` still observes the live `CFG.entropy_mode` value. If software changes the mode from `EntropyModeEdn` to `EntropyModeNone` without resetting the IP, the next refresh can behave as though the mode changed mid-session instead of preserving the original EDN-backed configuration.

## Affected Function
This affects the KMAC `kmac_entropy` entropy refresh and reseed path that supplies entropy to the SHA3/KMAC datapath.

## Trigger Condition
Configure `kmac_entropy` to use EDN entropy, assert `entropy_ready`, let it complete an initial seed or hash-related entropy cycle, and then, without resetting the KMAC IP, rewrite `CFG.entropy_mode` to `EntropyModeNone` before requesting another entropy refresh.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's silicon_creator mask ROM stores a small table of RSA public keys for boot signature verification. Whether each built-in key may be used is controlled by the One-Time Programmable (OTP) configuration item `CREATOR_SW_CFG_KEY_IS_VALID`, which stores one byte-sized hardened boolean validity entry per key. In the current two-key configuration, only the first key is enabled in OTP.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the mask ROM RSA key lookup path in `sigverify_rsa_key_get()`, which selects a built-in boot verification key from a requested key ID.

## Expected Behavior
If the requested key ID matches a built-in RSA key, `sigverify_rsa_key_get()` should return that key only when the corresponding `CREATOR_SW_CFG_KEY_IS_VALID` OTP entry marks it as enabled. If the key exists in the ROM table but its OTP validity entry marks it invalid, the lookup should fail with a bad-key result and should not return the key through the output pointer.

## Actual Behavior
At the buggy revision, a built-in RSA key is accepted solely because its key ID matches an entry in the ROM table. The OTP validity setting is ignored, so a key that is disabled in `CREATOR_SW_CFG_KEY_IS_VALID` is still returned as a usable boot verification key.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when software requests a key ID for a key that is present in the mask ROM key table but disabled by `CREATOR_SW_CFG_KEY_IS_VALID`. In the current two-key setup, requesting the second built-in RSA key should fail because only the first key is enabled in OTP, but the buggy code still accepts the second key.

problem_statement:
## Description
The Flash Controller (`flash_ctrl`) does not include all sensitive flash information pages in its Return Material Authorization (RMA) entry handling. When the life cycle controller requests RMA entry, `flash_ctrl` uses a hardware-managed sanitization path before the transition completes. The current implementation already handles `owner_seed_info`, but `creator_seed_info` and the isolated information page are not handled the same way.

## Expected Behavior
During RMA entry, `creator_seed_info` and the isolated information page must be treated like `owner_seed_info`: the RMA-phase hardware configuration must allow the controller to read, program, and erase those pages, and the RMA wipe sequence must include them so they are erased before RMA entry completes.

## Actual Behavior
During RMA entry, `owner_seed_info` is covered by the hardware RMA configuration and wipe sequence, but `creator_seed_info` and the isolated information page are omitted. As a result, sensitive data can remain in those pages after the device enters RMA.

## Affected Function
This affects the Flash Controller (`flash_ctrl`) RMA configuration for flash information pages, specifically the RMA access attributes and wipe coverage for `creator_seed_info` and the isolated information page.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when the life cycle controller requests RMA entry on a device that stores sensitive data in `creator_seed_info` or the isolated information page. In that case, the controller enters its normal RMA sanitization flow, but those pages are not included in the hardware-managed erase path.

resolved_issues.title: [rstmgr] Confusing rst_ni / clk_i definition
resolved_issues.body:
At the moment, the ast POR signal is fed through the `rst_ni` port. 
This POR is then synchronized and used locally. 

This means `rst_ni` cannot be used locally within `rstmgr`, however the same does not apply to `clk_i`.
This usage is confusing and error prone, and in fact has caused a bug on [this line](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/top_earlgrey/ip/rstmgr/rtl/autogen/rstmgr.sv#L106)

`rstmgr` is told by top level to use the `io_div4` clock, but locally hardwires its internal reset to one that is synchronous to `io_div2`.  

What we should instead do is bring in POR through another `intermodule` signal, and free up `rstmgr.rst_ni` to be directly driven through conventional means. That way the definition of `clk_i` and `rst_ni` will be consistent and less prone to error in the future.

problem_statement:
## Description
The Reset Manager (`rstmgr`) handles the power-on reset (POR) input and generates reset signals for multiple clock domains. In the affected top-level integration, the top-level POR signal is routed through `rstmgr.rst_ni`, even though `rst_ni` is also treated as the module reset for logic clocked by `clk_i`. This makes the meanings of `rst_ni` and `clk_i` inconsistent inside the `rstmgr` always-on instance.

## Actual Behavior
When `rstmgr` is configured so that `clk_i` uses the `io_div4` clock, some internal logic that runs on `clk_i` still uses a reset path synchronized to `io_div2`. During release from POR, `clk_i`-domain state can therefore leave reset according to the `io_div2` synchronization rather than on a `clk_i` / `io_div4` boundary.

## Expected Behavior
`rstmgr.rst_ni` should behave as the conventional module reset for logic clocked by `clk_i`, while POR should be delivered through a separate POR input. When `clk_i` is driven by `io_div4`, logic inside `rstmgr` that runs on `clk_i` must only be released by a reset that is synchronous to that same `io_div4` / `clk_i` domain.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered during POR release when the top-level integration feeds POR through `rst_ni` and configures `clk_i` to use `io_div4`, while the internal reset path for `clk_i`-domain logic remains synchronized to `io_div2`.

## Implementation Constraint
The fix should expose a POR-specific reset/input path distinct from the regular clk_i-domain module reset. Any new interface related to power-on reset should include the keyword `por`. Logic clocked by clk_i must only be released by a reset edge aligned to clk_i.

title: [tlul_adapter_sram] Fix minor bugs in byte write logic
body:
Split out from #7218.

----------------------

This fixes a few bugs in the byte write logic and adds a workaround for potential RAW hazards that can occur when the byte write logic is employed together with `prim_ram_1p_scr`.

This workaround should be removed once the DV environment of `sram_ctrl` is able to handle these corner cases (#7461).

Signed-off-by: Michael Schaffner <msf@google.com>

---------------------------------------------------

This makes use of the topgen feature added in #7267 in order to address #4709. I.e., the SRAM primitives are moved into the `sram_ctrl` IP, and the corresponding memory configurations in the toplevel Hjson are moved into the comportable IP instance entries.

resolved_issues.title: [sram_ctrl] Need to handle additional RAW hazards due to byte write handling
resolved_issues.body:
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/7218 updates the `sram_ctrl` to include the scrambled RAM primitive and the `tlul_adapter_sram`, and turns on all bus integrity-related features. Since the bus integrity scheme requires additional read-modify-write operations in case of partial writes, new RAW hazard conditions are introduced which the DV environment cannot handle at the moment.

As a workaround, the logic inside `tlul_sram_byte` currently inserts an idle cycle after a partial write operation such that these additional RAW hazards cannot occur.

We should discuss whether it is ok to leave that HW workaround in place, effectively reducing the throughput of partial writes even further, or whether the DV environment should be extended to handle the additional RAW hazard conditions.

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace (+submodules)
cd /home/opentitan
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx
git checkout 7d2e9949de35d9f9dc2a1d448051a7624e372697
git submodule update --init --recursive

# Stage 2: install repository apt dependencies (if present)
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
if [[ -f apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing apt dependencies from apt-requirements.txt"
  cp apt-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  sed -i -e '/^$/d' -e '/^#/d' -e 's/#.*//' /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  if [[ -s /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
    apt-get update
    xargs -r apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends < /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  else
    echo "[INFO] apt-requirements.txt is empty after filtering comments"
  fi
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[WARN] apt-requirements.txt not found at 7d2e9949de35d9f9dc2a1d448051a7624e372697; skipping repo-specific apt install"
fi

# Stage 3: install project-specific Python dependencies from the checked-out repo
if [[ -f python-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Python deps from python-requirements.txt"
  python -m pip install -U pip "setuptools<66.0.0"
  cp python-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
  python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re

path = Path("/tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt")
lines = []
for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    stripped = line.strip()
    if stripped in {
        "types-dataclasses",
        "types-pkg_resources",
    }:
        continue
    line = re.sub(r'(#egg=[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\s+[<>=!~].*', r'\1', line)
    lines.append(line)
path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
PY
  python -m pip install -r /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt --no-warn-script-location
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[ERROR] python-requirements.txt not found at 7d2e9949de35d9f9dc2a1d448051a7624e372697"
  exit 1
fi

# Stage 4: install RISC-V toolchain + Verible, then persist their PATH
if [[ -f util/get-toolchain.py ]]; then
  toolchain_version=""
  if [[ -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
    toolchain_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
  fi

  echo "[INFO] Installing RISC-V toolchain via util/get-toolchain.py"
  if [[ -n "$toolchain_version" ]]; then
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update -r "$toolchain_version"
  else
    echo "[WARN] RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION not found; falling back to util/get-toolchain.py defaults"
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update
  fi
else
  echo "[WARN] util/get-toolchain.py not found at 7d2e9949de35d9f9dc2a1d448051a7624e372697; skipping RISC-V toolchain install"
fi

verible_version=""
if [[ -f hw/tool_requirements.py ]]; then
  verible_version="$(python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

ns = {}
exec(Path("hw/tool_requirements.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), ns)
reqs = ns.get("__TOOL_REQUIREMENTS__", {})
entry = reqs.get("verible", "")
if isinstance(entry, dict):
    print(entry.get("min_version", ""))
elif isinstance(entry, str):
    print(entry)
PY
)"
fi
if [[ -z "$verible_version" && -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
  verible_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG VERIBLE_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
fi

if [[ -n "$verible_version" ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Verible ${verible_version}"
  rm -rf /tools/verible
  mkdir -p /tools/verible
  curl -f -Ls -o /tmp/verible.tar.gz \
    "https://github.com/chipsalliance/verible/releases/download/${verible_version}/verible-${verible_version}-linux-static-x86_64.tar.gz"
  tar -C /tools/verible -xf /tmp/verible.tar.gz --strip-components=1
  rm -f /tmp/verible.tar.gz
else
  echo "[WARN] Unable to determine Verible version from hw/tool_requirements.py or util/container/Dockerfile"
fi

cat > /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh <<'EOF'
for d in /tools/riscv/bin /tools/verible/bin; do
  if [ -d "$d" ]; then
    export PATH="$d:$PATH"
  fi
done
true

problem_statement:
## Description
`tlul_sram_byte`, the byte-write helper used by `tlul_adapter_sram` when TileLink Uncached Lightweight (TL-UL) integrity handling is enabled, does not preserve the correct semantics for partial writes. When a `PutPartialData` request updates only part of a 32-bit word, the module performs an internal read-modify-write sequence to regenerate integrity bits. For a sub-word write that targets a byte lane inside the word, the memory-facing transactions are not consistently converted into accesses to the containing aligned word, and the completion returned to the upstream TL-UL host can report the internal full-word transfer size instead of the original request size.

## Expected Behavior
A partial write must be executed internally as a read-modify-write of the containing aligned 32-bit word. The memory-facing read and write should both use the aligned word address, use the full-word access size, and cover all byte lanes of that word. The writeback data should combine the previously stored word with the updated byte lanes from the original request. The TL-UL response returned to the host must preserve the original request size rather than the internal full-word transfer size.

## Actual Behavior
For a partial write, the internal read-modify-write path can retain sub-word request semantics instead of switching fully to aligned full-word semantics. This means the downstream memory-side access can use the incoming byte address or request size instead of the containing word address and full-word size, and the response observed by the TL-UL host can expose the internal full-word size rather than the original partial-write size.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the integrity-enabled partial-write handling in `tlul_sram_byte`, which is used by the byte-write path of `tlul_adapter_sram`.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered by a `PutPartialData` request whose mask does not cover the entire 32-bit word, especially a single-byte or other sub-word write to a non-word-aligned address within that word.

title: [top, keymgr, kmac] Ensure masking consistency between keymgr/kmac
body:
- Fixes #7149
- Previously, if kmac disabled masking, keymgr would error out during
  operation because one of the return slots from kmac is always '0'.
- This PR teaches keymgr that kmac may not be masked and to behave
  accordingly.
- In order to ensure the two sides do not get out of sync, the kmac
  mask parameter is sent over via regular IOs to keymgr for a consistency
  check.  However this IO is not used directly by the logic anywhere.
  This is because if boundary optimization or constant propagation were
  ever disabled, the IO port would effectively become the single point
  where keymgr masking could also be disabled.  This would not be a good
  thing and the IO is used for checking only.

Signed-off-by: Timothy Chen <timothytim@google.com>

resolved_issues.title: [kmac/keymgr] kmac masking dependency and keymgr correctness
resolved_issues.body:
It turns out that if kmac masking is not enabled (via parameter), keymgr can't function at all because one of the shares coming back is always 0.  

This causes keymgr to fire off its kmac data invalid check and just completely disables the key manager.
We probably need to pass the same parameter information to keymgr also to ensure that the two sides are consistent.

This also brings up the question if this kind of data error really should be considered "fault" in the keymgr.  It's probably to leave as is right now, but could be difficult to debug if we ever run into it. It might be better for keymgr to disclose more fine grained errors.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan Key Manager IP (`keymgr`) consumes derived values from the KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) application interface. When KMAC masking is enabled, that interface returns two shares. When KMAC masking is disabled, the interface returns the effective derived value in share 0 and drives share 1 to all zeroes. `keymgr` currently still validates the response as if both shares must contain valid masked data, so an unmasked KMAC response can be misclassified as invalid output.

## Expected Behavior
`keymgr` must interpret KMAC output using the same masking assumption as the KMAC IP. In builds where KMAC masking is disabled, a KMAC response with a valid value in share 0 and all zeroes in share 1 must be accepted as valid. After the key manager has been initialized, an advance operation that receives such a response should complete successfully and move the key manager to its next working state instead of reporting an invalid-output error.

## Actual Behavior
With KMAC masking disabled, `keymgr` treats share 1 being all zeroes as a bad KMAC result. In the failing case above, the advance operation fails with an invalid-output condition and the key manager transitions to its disabled state instead of continuing normal operation.

## Affected Module
This bug affects the OpenTitan Key Manager IP (`keymgr`), specifically the control logic that validates KMAC application-response data during key-manager advance operations.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when OpenTitan is built with KMAC masking disabled and `keymgr` receives an unmasked KMAC response: share 0 contains a valid derived value and share 1 is zero. A concrete reproducer is an advance operation issued after key-manager initialization under that configuration.

problem_statement:
The OpenTitan always-on timer (AON timer) wakeup request path does not satisfy the power manager (`pwrmgr`) wakeup protocol. The power manager does not latch incoming wakeup requests, so each wakeup source must hold its wakeup output high until software acknowledges the event by clearing that source's recorded wakeup cause.

For the AON timer, when its wakeup threshold expires while sleep mode is active, the timer records the wakeup cause and asserts its wakeup request. If the system then exits sleep because of that wakeup before software clears the AON timer wakeup cause register (`WKUP_CAUSE`), the wakeup request must remain asserted. It should deassert only after software clears `WKUP_CAUSE`. The observed bug is that the AON timer wakeup request can drop as soon as sleep mode is exited, even though the wakeup cause is still set and software has not acknowledged it.

body:
An update error in a particular field should only prevent the update of that field. Updates to other fields should still be applied.

This fixes lowRISC/OpenTitan#7417.

resolved_issues.title: [Shadow_reg] Unify the shadow reg field update error behavior
resolved_issues.body:
Hi Michael and Pirmin,

With AES and ALERT_HANDLER both have shadow registers, I found the have slight different behaviors:

1). For AES, the shadow registers are extended as registers: https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/aes/rtl/aes_core.sv#L498

2). For ALERT_HANDLER, shadow registers are extended by each field:
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/alert_handler/rtl/alert_handler_reg_top.sv#L3512

So these two behavior swill cause the following difference:
If we have a shadow register (Reg_A) with two fields (Field_A, Field_B), both field 1 bits. Reset value `b00`.
Sequence:
a). First write with data `b11`
b). Second write with data `b01`
Both method 1) and 2) will trigger update alert, but read out this register before reset is different.
1). Will read out value `b00`
2). Will read out value `b01`, because field (Field_A) does not have update error, only Field_B has update error.

If possible, could we unify the behavior so it is easier for DV to automate it? Currently DV implemented as method 1), but happy to adopt with any design change.

Thanks,
Cindy

+  output key_len_e  key_len_o,
+  output logic      manual_operation_o,
+  output logic      force_zero_masks_o,
+
+  // Alerts
+  output logic err_update_o,
+  output logic err_storage_o,
+
+  // Bus interface
+  input  aes_reg2hw_ctrl_shadowed_reg_t reg2hw_ctrl_i,
+  output aes_hw2reg_ctrl_shadowed_reg_t hw2reg_ctrl_o
+);
+
+  // Signals
+  ctrl_reg_t ctrl_wd;
+  aes_mode_e mode;
+  key_len_e  key_len;
+  logic      err_update_operation;
+  logic      err_update_mode;
+  logic      err_update_key_len;
+  logic      err_update_manual_operation;
+  logic      err_update_force_zero_masks;
+  logic      err_storage_operation;
+  logic      err_storage_mode;
+  logic      err_storage_key_len;
+  logic      err_storage_manual_operation;
+  logic      err_storage_force_zero_masks;
+
+  // Unused signals
+  logic unused_force_zero_masks;
+
+  // Get and forward write enable. Writes are only allowed if the module is idle.
+  assign qe_o = reg2hw_ctrl_i.operation.qe & reg2hw_ctrl_i.mode.qe &
+      reg2hw_ctrl_i.key_len.qe & reg2hw_ctrl_i.manual_operation.qe &
+      reg2hw_ctrl_i.force_zero_masks.qe;
+
+  // Get and resolve values from register interface.
+  assign ctrl_wd.operation = aes_op_e'(reg2hw_ctrl_i.operation.q);
+
+  assign mode = aes_mode_e'(reg2hw_ctrl_i.mode.q);
+  always_comb begin : mode_get
+    unique case (mode)
+      AES_ECB: ctrl_wd.mode = AES_ECB;
+      AES_CBC: ctrl_wd.mode = AES_CBC;
+      AES_CFB: ctrl_wd.mode = AES_CFB;
+      AES_OFB: ctrl_wd.mode = AES_OFB;
+      AES_CTR: ctrl_wd.mode = AES_CTR;
+      default: ctrl_wd.mode = AES_NONE; // unsupported values are mapped to AES_NONE
+    endcase
+  end
+
+  assign key_len = key_len_e'(reg2hw_ctrl_i.key_len.q);
+  always_comb begin : key_len_get
+    unique case (key_len)
+      AES_128: ctrl_wd.key_len = AES_128;
+      AES_256: ctrl_wd.key_len = AES_256;
+      AES_192: ctrl_wd.key_len = AES192Enable ? AES_192 : AES_256;
+      default: ctrl_wd.key_len = AES_256; // unsupported values are mapped to AES_256
+    endcase
+  end
+
+  assign ctrl_wd.manual_operation = reg2hw_ctrl_i.manual_operation.q;
+
+  // SecAllowForcingMasks forbids forcing the masks. Forcing the masks to zero is only
+  // useful for SCA.
+  assign ctrl_wd.force_zero_masks = SecAllowForcingMasks ? reg2hw_ctrl_i.force_zero_masks.q : 1'b0;
+  assign unused_force_zero_masks = SecAllowForcingMasks ? 1'b0 : reg2hw_ctrl_i.force_zero_masks.q;
+
+  // Instantiate one shadowed register primitive per field. An update error in a field should
+  // only prevent the update of the affected field.
+  prim_subreg_shadow #(
+    .DW      ($bits(aes_op_e)),
+    .SwAccess(prim_subreg_pkg::SwAccessWO),
+    .RESVAL  (AES_CTRL_SHADOWED_OPERATION_RESVAL)
+  ) u_ctrl_reg_shadowed_operation (
+    .clk_i,
+    .rst_ni,
+    .re         (reg2hw_ctrl_i.operation.re),
+    .we         (we_i),
+    .wd         (ctrl_wd.operation),
+    .de         (1'b0),
+    .d          ('0),
+    .qe         (),
+    .q          (hw2reg_ctrl_o.operation.d),
+    .qs         (),
+    .err_update (err_update_operation),
+    .err_storage(err_storage_operation)
+  );
+
+  prim_subreg_shadow #(
+    .DW      ($bits(aes_mode_e)),
+    .SwAccess(prim_subreg_pkg::SwAccessWO),
+    .RESVAL  (AES_CTRL_SHADOWED_MODE_RESVAL)
+  ) u_ctrl_reg_shadowed_mode (
+    .clk_i,
+    .rst_ni,
+    .re         (reg2hw_ctrl_i.mode.re),
+    .we         (we_i),
+    .wd         ({ctrl_wd.mode}),
+    .de         (1'b0),
+    .d          ('0),
+    .qe         (),
+    .q          (hw2reg_ctrl_o.mode.d),
+    .qs         (),
+    .err_update (err_update_mode),
+    .err_storage(err_storage_mode)
+  );
+
+  prim_subreg_shadow #(
+    .DW      ($bits(key_len_e)),
+    .SwAccess(prim_subreg_pkg::SwAccessWO),
+    .RESVAL  (AES_CTRL_SHADOWED_KEY_LEN_RESVAL)
+  ) u_ctrl_reg_shadowed_key_len (
+    .clk_i,
+    .rst_ni,
+    .re         (reg2hw_ctrl_i.key_len.re),
+    .we         (we_i),
+    .wd         ({ctrl_wd.key_len}),
+    .de         (1'b0),
+    .d          ('0),
+    .qe         (),
+    .q          (hw2reg_ctrl_o.key_len.d),
+    .qs         (),
+    .err_update (err_update_key_len),
+    .err_storage(err_storage_key_len)
+  );
+
+  prim_subreg_shadow #(
+    .DW      (1),
+    .SwAccess(prim_subreg_pkg::SwAccessWO),
+    .RESVAL  (AES_CTRL_SHADOWED_MANUAL_OPERATION_RESVAL)
+  ) u_ctrl_reg_shadowed_manual_operation (
+    .clk_i,
+    .rst_ni,
+    .re         (reg2hw_ctrl_i.manual_operation.re),
+    .we         (we_i),
+    .wd         (ctrl_wd.manual_operation),
+    .de         (1'b0),
+    .d          ('0),
+    .qe         (),
+    .q          (hw2reg_ctrl_o.manual_operation.d),
+    .qs         (),
+    .err_update (err_update_manual_operation),
+    .err_storage(err_storage_manual_operation)
+  );
+
+  prim_subreg_shadow #(
+    .DW      (1),
+    .SwAccess(prim_subreg_pkg::SwAccessWO),
+    .RESVAL  (AES_CTRL_SHADOWED_FORCE_ZERO_MASKS_RESVAL)
+  ) u_ctrl_reg_shadowed_force_zero_masks (
+    .clk_i,
+    .rst_ni,
+    .re         (reg2hw_ctrl_i.force_zero_masks.re),
+    .we         (we_i),
+    .wd         (ctrl_wd.force_zero_masks),
+    .de         (1'b0),
+    .d          ('0),
+    .qe         (),
+    .q          (hw2reg_ctrl_o.force_zero_masks.d),
+    .qs         (),
+    .err_update (err_update_force_zero_masks),
+    .err_storage(err_storage_force_zero_masks)
+  );
+
+  // Collect alerts.
+  assign err_update_o = err_update_operation | err_update_mode | err_update_key_len |
+      err_update_manual_operation | err_update_force_zero_masks;
+  assign err_storage_o = err_storage_operation | err_storage_mode | err_storage_key_len |
+      err_storage_manual_operation | err_storage_force_zero_masks;
+
+  // Generate shorter references.
+  // Doing that here as opposed to in aes_core avoids several Verilator lint errors.
+  assign operation_o        = aes_op_e'(hw2reg_ctrl_o.operation.d);
+  assign mode_o             = aes_mode_e'(hw2reg_ctrl_o.mode.d);
+  assign key_len_o          = key_len_e'(hw2reg_ctrl_o.key_len.d);
+  assign manual_operation_o = hw2reg_ctrl_o.manual_operation.d;
+  assign force_zero_masks_o = hw2reg_ctrl_o.force_zero_masks.d;
+
+endmodule

prepare_script:
#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace (+submodules)
cd /home/opentitan
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx
git checkout 84b7d1be2cb09a204c3d34b8b3d0cb03878a94c2
git submodule update --init --recursive

# Stage 2: install repository apt dependencies (if present)
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
if [[ -f apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing apt dependencies from apt-requirements.txt"
  cp apt-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  sed -i -e '/^$/d' -e '/^#/d' -e 's/#.*//' /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  if [[ -s /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
    apt-get update
    xargs -r apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends < /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  else
    echo "[INFO] apt-requirements.txt is empty after filtering comments"
  fi
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[WARN] apt-requirements.txt not found at 84b7d1be2cb09a204c3d34b8b3d0cb03878a94c2; skipping repo-specific apt install"
fi

# Stage 3: install project-specific Python dependencies from the checked-out repo
if [[ -f python-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Python deps from python-requirements.txt"
  python -m pip install -U pip "setuptools<66.0.0"
  cp python-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
  python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re

path = Path("/tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt")
lines = []
for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    stripped = line.strip()
    if stripped in {
        "types-dataclasses",
        "types-pkg_resources",
    }:
        continue
    line = re.sub(r'(#egg=[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\s+[<>=!~].*', r'\1', line)
    lines.append(line)
path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
PY
  python -m pip install -r /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt --no-warn-script-location
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[ERROR] python-requirements.txt not found at 84b7d1be2cb09a204c3d34b8b3d0cb03878a94c2"
  exit 1
fi

# Stage 4: install RISC-V toolchain + Verible, then persist their PATH
if [[ -f util/get-toolchain.py ]]; then
  toolchain_version=""
  if [[ -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
    toolchain_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
  fi

  echo "[INFO] Installing RISC-V toolchain via util/get-toolchain.py"
  if [[ -n "$toolchain_version" ]]; then
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update -r "$toolchain_version"
  else
    echo "[WARN] RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION not found; falling back to util/get-toolchain.py defaults"
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update
  fi
else
  echo "[WARN] util/get-toolchain.py not found at 84b7d1be2cb09a204c3d34b8b3d0cb03878a94c2; skipping RISC-V toolchain install"
fi

verible_version=""
if [[ -f hw/tool_requirements.py ]]; then
  verible_version="$(python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

ns = {}
exec(Path("hw/tool_requirements.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), ns)
reqs = ns.get("__TOOL_REQUIREMENTS__", {})
entry = reqs.get("verible", "")
if isinstance(entry, dict):
    print(entry.get("min_version", ""))
elif isinstance(entry, str):
    print(entry)
PY
)"
fi
if [[ -z "$verible_version" && -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
  verible_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG VERIBLE_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
fi

if [[ -n "$verible_version" ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Verible ${verible_version}"
  rm -rf /tools/verible
  mkdir -p /tools/verible
  curl -f -Ls -o /tmp/verible.tar.gz \
    "https://github.com/chipsalliance/verible/releases/download/${verible_version}/verible-${verible_version}-linux-static-x86_64.tar.gz"
  tar -C /tools/verible -xf /tmp/verible.tar.gz --strip-components=1
  rm -f /tmp/verible.tar.gz
else
  echo "[WARN] Unable to determine Verible version from hw/tool_requirements.py or util/container/Dockerfile"
fi

cat > /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh <<'EOF'
for d in /tools/riscv/bin /tools/verible/bin; do
  [ -d "$d" ] && export PATH="$d:$PATH"
done
# Keep the sourced helper successful even when an optional tool directory is absent.
true
EOF

if ! grep -q "/etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" /etc/opentitan_bash_env; then
  echo "source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" >> /etc/opentitan_bash_env
fi
source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh

if ! python -m pip show edalize fusesoc hjson >/dev/null; then
  echo "[WARN] Some Python DV dependencies are not visible after Stage 4"
fi
if command -v riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[INFO] RISC-V toolchain ready: $(riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc --version | head -n1)"
else
  echo "[WARN] riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc not found after Stage 4"
fi
if command -v verible-verilog-lint >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[INFO] Verible ready: $(verible-verilog-lint --version | head -n1)"
else
  echo "[WARN] verible-verilog-lint not found after Stage 4"
fi
problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan AES IP's `CTRL_SHADOWED` register is a shadowed control register in the AES core. A shadowed register is programmed by writing the same value twice; if the two writes do not match, the AES IP must raise an update error alert. The bug affects how `CTRL_SHADOWED` behaves when only one field differs between the two shadow writes.

## Expected Behavior
While AES is idle, if software performs the two-write update of `CTRL_SHADOWED` and only `MANUAL_OPERATION` differs between the first and second write, the AES IP must still raise the update error alert, but only the mismatching field may be rejected. The fields that matched in both writes, specifically `OPERATION`, `MODE`, and `KEY_LEN` in this scenario, must commit to their new values. A read of `CTRL_SHADOWED` before reset must therefore show the newly written values for `OPERATION`, `MODE`, and `KEY_LEN`, while `MANUAL_OPERATION` remains at its previously committed value.

## Actual Behavior
In the current AES implementation, a mismatch in a single `CTRL_SHADOWED` field causes the entire register update to be discarded. The alert is raised, but a later read returns the old value for fields that matched in both writes instead of preserving their new values.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when the AES block is idle and software performs the normal two-write update of `CTRL_SHADOWED` with matching values for `OPERATION`, `MODE`, and `KEY_LEN`, but a different value for `MANUAL_OPERATION` in the second write.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan key manager (`keymgr`) control finite-state machine mishandles an in-flight `OpAdvance` operation that performs the initial transition from `StReset` to `StInit`. If the life cycle controller disables the key manager by deasserting the key manager enable signal (`keymgr_en`) before that initial advance has finished, the block can abandon initialization and enter an invalid state while still reporting the advance as successful.

## Expected Behavior
If `keymgr_en` drops while the `StReset` to `StInit` advance is still in progress, that advance must be marked as an error, not as a successful completion. In this situation, the key manager may move to `StInvalid` and wipe key material because it has been disabled, but software-visible `OP_STATUS` must report that the in-flight operation failed.

## Actual Behavior
When `keymgr_en` is deasserted during an in-progress `StReset` to `StInit` advance, the key manager updates its state to `StInvalid` and wipes keys, yet `OP_STATUS` can still report success and no operation error is recorded.

## Trigger Condition
Start an `OpAdvance` from `StReset`, then disable the key manager before the transition reaches `StInit`. The bug is specific to the initial reset-to-init advance while that operation is still in flight.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan Key Manager sideload key controller provides hardware keys directly to downstream IP blocks such as AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code), and OTBN (OpenTitan Big Number Accelerator) without exposing the key material to software. A per-destination sideload clear request is intended to invalidate only the selected destination's sideload key, not every sideloaded key held by the controller.

## Expected Behavior
If multiple sideload destinations currently hold valid keys, clearing one destination must invalidate only that destination. For example, when both AES and OTBN have valid sideload keys, issuing sideload_clear for OTBN must make the OTBN sideload key invalid while the AES sideload key remains valid.

## Actual Behavior
A clear request for one sideload destination can also make another destination lose its valid sideload key. In the reported case, after both AES and OTBN hold valid sideload keys, issuing sideload_clear for OTBN can cause the AES sideload key to become invalid as well.

## Affected Function
The bug is in the Key Manager sideload key control logic that maintains per-destination sideload key validity for the AES, KMAC, and OTBN outputs.

## Trigger Condition
The failure occurs when at least two sideload destinations have been loaded with valid keys and software issues a targeted clear for only one of them, such as clearing OTBN while AES still holds a valid sideload key.

class keymgr_storage_err_block_vseq extends keymgr_base_vseq;
  `uvm_object_utils(keymgr_storage_err_block_vseq)
  `uvm_object_new

  virtual task body();
    dv_base_reg csr;
    uvm_reg_data_t committed_val;
    uvm_reg_data_t poison_val;
    uvm_reg_data_t write_val;
    uvm_reg_data_t after_val;
    string alert_name;

    do_op_before_init = 1'b0;
    dut_init();

    csr = ral.reseed_interval_shadowed;
    csr_peek(.ptr(csr), .value(committed_val), .kind(BkdrRegPathRtlCommitted));
    poison_val = committed_val ^ 16'h1;
    write_val = committed_val ^ 16'h55aa;
    if (write_val == committed_val || write_val == poison_val) begin
      write_val = committed_val + 16'h2;
    end

    `uvm_info(`gfn, $sformatf("Inject storage error into %0s: old=0x%0h poison=0x%0h new=0x%0h",
                              csr.get_name(), committed_val, poison_val, write_val), UVM_MEDIUM)

    csr_poke(.ptr(csr), .value(poison_val), .kind(BkdrRegPathRtlCommitted), .predict(0));
    cfg.clk_rst_vif.wait_clks(2);

    alert_name = csr.get_storage_err_alert_name();
    `DV_SPINWAIT(while (!cfg.m_alert_agent_cfg[alert_name].vif.get_alert())
                   cfg.clk_rst_vif.wait_clks(1);,
                 $sformatf("%0s storage_err alert not detected", csr.get_name()))
    `DV_SPINWAIT(cfg.m_alert_agent_cfg[alert_name].vif.wait_ack_complete();,
                 $sformatf("timeout for alert:%0s", alert_name))

    csr_wr(.ptr(csr), .value(write_val), .predict(0));
    cfg.clk_rst_vif.wait_clks(2);
    csr_peek(.ptr(csr), .value(after_val), .kind(BkdrRegPathRtlCommitted));

    `DV_CHECK_EQ(after_val, poison_val,
                 $sformatf("%0s updated after storage error: poison=0x%0h after=0x%0h write=0x%0h",
                           csr.get_name(), poison_val, after_val, write_val))

    dut_init();
  endtask
endclass
SV

if ! grep -q 'keymgr_storage_err_block_vseq' "${SEQ_LIST}"; then
  printf '\n`include "%s"\n' "${SEQ_FILE}" >> "${SEQ_LIST}"
fi

set +e
timeout 1800 python util/dvsim/dvsim.py \
  hw/ip/keymgr/dv/keymgr_sim_cfg.hjson \
  -i keymgr_shadow_reg_errors \
  -t vcs \

set -e

if [ "${build_rc}" -ne 0 ] || [ ! -f "${SIMV}" ] || [ ! -f "${ENV_VARS}" ]; then
  report_result FAIL
  exit 1
fi

remaining=$((1800 - SECONDS))
if [ "${remaining}" -le 0 ]; then
  report_result FAIL
  exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "${RUN_DIR}"

set +e
timeout "${remaining}" bash -lc "
  set -e
  set -a
  source '${ENV_VARS}'
  set +a
  export dv_root=/home/opentitan/hw/dv
  export proj_root=/home/opentitan
  cd '${RUN_DIR}'
  '${SIMV}' \
    +en_scb=0 \
    +UVM_NO_RELNOTES \
    +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_LOW \
    -licqueue \
    -ucli \
    -do /home/opentitan/hw/dv/tools/sim.tcl \
    +ntb_random_seed=1 \
    -assert nopostproc \
    +UVM_TESTNAME=keymgr_base_test \
    +UVM_TEST_SEQ=keymgr_storage_err_block_vseq
" | tee "${RUN_LOG}"
run_rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}

if [ "${run_rc}" -eq 0 ] && grep -q "TEST PASSED CHECKS" "${RUN_LOG}"; then

fi

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan Key Manager uses shadowed Control and Status Registers (CSRs) for critical configuration fields. A shadowed CSR keeps redundant internal copies so that a storage mismatch can be detected as a fault. In the Key Manager, `RESEED_INTERVAL_SHADOWED` is one such register.

## Expected Behavior
If `RESEED_INTERVAL_SHADOWED` is already in a storage-error condition because its redundant copies no longer match, a later software write to that same CSR must be blocked. The register value exposed through the CSR interface must remain unchanged after the write attempt.

## Actual Behavior
After corrupting one internal copy of `RESEED_INTERVAL_SHADOWED` so that the register enters the storage-error condition, a normal software write to `RESEED_INTERVAL_SHADOWED` can still change the register value.

## Affected Function and Trigger
The bug affects the shadowed-register handling used by the Key Manager, as observed on `RESEED_INTERVAL_SHADOWED`. It is triggered when one redundant copy of that shadowed CSR is corrupted to create a storage mismatch, the storage error is detected, and software then writes a new value to the same CSR.

resolved_issues.body:
Right now rv_dm's life cycle gating is fairly weak

- one location is the instruction fetch from rv_dm rom through tlul_adapter_sram
- the other is in the pinmux to ensure rv_dm tap cannot be selected.

This should be enhanced further as follows:
- use life cycle to gate debug rom response
- use life cycle to gate valid coming from sba access
- use life cycle to gate ready returning to sba access

This will ensure that a defeat of any individual point does not allow debug functions to completely resume.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's RISC-V Debug Module (`rv_dm`) does not fully enforce life cycle based debug disablement on its System Bus Access (SBA) path. SBA lets a debugger issue memory-mapped accesses over the TL-UL (TileLink Uncached Lightweight) bus through the Debug Module Interface (DMI). The design relies in part on external JTAG Test Access Port (TAP) selection controls to keep debug traffic out of `rv_dm`, but the module should still remain non-operational if those controls are bypassed and DMI requests reach the block while hardware debug is disabled.

## Expected Behavior
When the life cycle hardware debug enable is Off, `rv_dm` must not start any SBA transaction on its TL-UL host interface. If JTAG traffic carrying DMI commands still reaches `rv_dm` and a debugger attempts an SBA read or write, the module must not drive an outbound SBA request toward the system bus.

## Actual Behavior
The life cycle gating around the SBA path is too weak. Under debug-disabled life cycle conditions, JTAG/DMI activity can still trigger an SBA access and cause `rv_dm` to emit a TL-UL host-side SBA request. This means that defeating a single external gating point can partially restore debug functionality even though hardware debug is supposed to be disabled.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the `rv_dm` System Bus Access path, specifically the life cycle enforcement on the TL-UL host request side used for SBA operations.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when the life cycle controller has hardware debug disabled, but JTAG/TAP routing or another external gate is bypassed so that DMI commands still reach `rv_dm`, and an SBA read or write is attempted.

resolved_issues.title: [keymgr/dv] Fix a few issues in scb for LC disable

resolved_issues.title: [keymgr] last strb is 0 when LC turns off keymgr
resolved_issues.body:
@tjaychen 
usually `strb` is never 0 when the valid is high. We also have assertion to check that and I think KMAC TB probably never test the case that `strb` is valid with value 0.

When LC turns off keymgr in the middle of an operation, we will see the last `strb` is set to 0.
![Screen Shot 2021-08-24 at 10 54 44 AM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/49293026/130666192-58914373-3087-4323-84fd-a7efcdff6828.png)

Since this interacts with KMAC, we probably can't test this corner scenario in chip-level. If we do want to have this case in the keymgr side, we may need to test it at KMAC block-level TB as well.

cc @eunchan @udinator

--- a/hw/ip/keymgr/doc/_index.md
+++ b/hw/ip/keymgr/doc/_index.md
@@ -126,11 +126,34 @@ Upon `Disabled` entry, the working state is updated with KMAC computed random va
 This allows the software to keep the last valid sideload keys while preventing the system from further advancing the valid key.
 
 When advance and generate calls are invoked from this state, the outputs and keys are indiscriminately updated with randomly computed values.
+Key manager enters disabled state based on direct invocation by software:
+* Advance from `OwnerRootKey`
+* Disable operation
 
 ### Invalid
-`Invalid` state is entered whenever key manager is disabled through the [life cycle connection](#life-cycle-connection).
+`Invalid` state is entered whenever key manager is disabled through the [life cycle connection](#life-cycle-connection) or when an operation encounters a [fault](#faults-and-operational-faults) .
 Upon `Invalid` entry, both the working state and the sideload keys are wiped with entropy directly.
-Note, this is different from `Disabled` state entry, which updates with KMAC outputs.
+Note, this is different from `Disabled` state entry, which updates internal key with KMAC outputs but leaves sideload and software keys intact.
+
+#### Invalid Entry Wiping
+Since the life cycle controller can disable the key manager at any time, the key manager attempts to gracefully handle the wiping process.
+When the disable is seen, the key manager immediately begins wiping all keys (internal key, hardware sideload key, software key) with entropy.
+However, if an operation was already ongoing, the key manager waits for the transaction to complete gracefully before transitioning to invalid state.
+
+While waiting for the transaction to complete, the key manager continuously wipes all keys with entropy.
+
+### Invalid and Disabled State
+
+Note that `Invalid` and `Disabled` states are functionally equivalent.
+The main difference between the two is "how" the state was reached.
+
+`Disabled` state is reached through intentional software commands.
+While `Invalid` state is reached through life cycle disable or operational faults.
+
+This also means that only `Invalid` is a terminal state.
+If after entering `Disabled` life cycle is disabled or a fault is encountered, the same [invalid entry procedure](#Invalid) is followed to bring the system to a terminal `Invalid` state.
+
+If ever multiple conditions collide (a fault is detected at the same time software issues disable command), the `Invalid` entry path always takes precedence.
 
 ## Life Cycle Connection
 The function of the key manager is directly tied to the life cycle controller.
@@ -193,11 +216,32 @@ There are two categories of errors
 
 Two separate alerts are generated, one corresponding to each category above.
 
-In addition to the error code register, there is a separate {{< regref FAULT_STATUS >}} that captures the sources that caused `Invalid states` to assert.
-*  Command error - A non-one-hot command was issued from the key manager controller to the KMAC data interface. This is not possible by software and indicates a hardware fault.  This error can also happen if the KMCA data fsm gets into an invalid state.
-*  Kmac fsm error - The kmac fsm has transitioned into an error state.
-*  Kmac operation error - The kmac module has returned an error, this should never happen.
-*  Register file integrity error - The register file has encountered an integrity error.
+### Faults and Operational Faults
+
+The {{< regref FAULT_STATUS >}} register captures all faults that can occur within the key manager.
+Some of these faults can occur only when there is a key manager operation ongoing, other faults can happen at any time (for example register integrity faults or shadow storage faults).
+{{< regref FAULT_STATUS >}} captures all faults regardless of when they happen.
+
+The {{< regref ERR_CODE.INVALID_STATES >}} field represents the presence of **any** fault during a key manager operation.
+This means if a fault happens before or during an operation, it will be recognized as an operational fault and result in keymgr's transition to `Invalid` state.
+
+#### Example 1: Fault During Operation
+The key manager is running a generate operation and a non-onehot command was observed by the kmac interface.
+Since the non-onehot condition is a fault, it will be reflected in {{< regref FAULT_STATUS >}}.
+Since an operation was ongoing when this fault was seen, it will also be reflected in {{< regref ERR_CODE.INVALID_STATES >}}.
+This is considered an operational fault and begin transition to the `Invalid` [state](#invalid-entry-wiping).
+
+#### Example 2: Fault During Idle
+The key manager is NOT running an operation and is idle.
+During this time, a fault was observed on the regfile (shadow storage error) and FSM (control FSM integrity error).
+The faults will be reflected in {{< regref FAULT_STATUS >}}.
+However, since there was no ongoing key manager operation, the error is **not** reflected in {{< regref ERR_CODE.INVALID_STATES >}}.
+This is **not** considered an operational fault and the key manager will remain in its current state.
+
+#### Example 3: Operation after Fault Detection
+Continuing from the example above, assume now the key manager begins an operation.
+Since the key manager has previous encountered a fault, any operation now is considered an operational fault and will be reflected in {{< regref ERR_CODE.INVALID_STATES >}}.
+This is considered an operational fault and begin transition to the `Invalid` [state](#invalid-entry-wiping).
 
 
 ### Invalid Output
@@ -254,6 +298,7 @@ See the tables below for an enumeration.
 *  During `Initialized`, `CreatorRootKey`, `OwnerIntermediateKey` and `OwnerRootKey` states, a fault error causes the relevant key / outputs to be updated; however an operational error does not.
 *  During `Invalid` and `Disabled` states, the relevant key / outputs are updated regardless of the error.
 *  Only the relevant collateral is updated -> ie, advance / disable command leads to working key update, and generate command leads to software or sideload key update.
+*  During `Disabled` state, if life cycle is disabled or an operational fault is encountered, the key manager transitions to `Invalid` state, see [here](#invalid-and-disabled-state)

problem_statement:
## Description
The Key Manager (`keymgr`) IP can send an invalid final request beat on its KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) application interface when the life cycle controller (`lc_ctrl`) asynchronously disables `keymgr` during an operation that has already started.

## Expected Behavior
If the life cycle controller withdraws `keymgr_en` after a Key Manager advance or generate request has already been accepted, the in-flight KMAC request must remain protocol-valid until it finishes. In particular, on every cycle where the request `valid` signal is asserted, the byte strobe (`strb`) must be non-zero, including the final transfer beat.

## Actual Behavior
When `lc_ctrl` disables `keymgr` in the middle of an operation, the final KMAC request beat can be driven with `valid` high and `strb` equal to zero. This violates the KMAC application-interface contract.

## Affected Function
The bug affects the Key Manager IP's life-cycle-disable handling for in-flight advance and generate operations that are transmitting data to the KMAC application interface.

## Trigger Condition
Revoke `keymgr_en` asynchronously while the Key Manager is already busy with an accepted advance or generate operation, especially near the final transfer beat of the KMAC request.

resolved_issues.body:
A couple of things to look into and see if it is worth hardening

- the "[clear](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/alert_handler/rtl/alert_handler_esc_timer.sv#L160)" signal right now is not shadowed, which means it could potentially be glitched to skip all the escalation responses.  (@msfschaffner let me know if i misunderstood).

- when in "[terminal](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/alert_handler/rtl/alert_handler_esc_timer.sv#L261)" state all the escalation requests are turned off. Does it make sense when in terminal to just fire all escalations? This is not really that important since the liklihood of glitching into `Terminal` is low due to sparse encoding and redundant counters.

- Question - when escalation sender observes an [error](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/prim/rtl/prim_esc_sender.sv#L199) does it make sense to cycle back to idle, or should we progress to a state that would both request escalation forever and timeout on pings? The error observed might be a result of a glitch between escalation sender / receiver.  This is closely related to the alert clock/power boundary discussion.

problem_statement:
## Description
In the Alert Handler IP block, the per-class escalation-clear control/status registers (CSRs) are not protected by shadowed-register semantics. In OpenTitan, a shadowed register is only supposed to take effect after two identical writes, so a single transient or glitched bus write must not immediately trigger the protected action.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the Alert Handler per-class escalation-clear path for the class clear CSRs for Classes A through D, including the clear pulse generated for a class such as Class D.

## Expected Behavior
When a class clear CSR is writable, it should behave like a shadowed register: the first write should only stage the value, and hardware should emit a single class clear pulse only after a second matching write. A single write must not produce the clear pulse.

## Actual Behavior
A single write to a class clear CSR immediately emits the class clear pulse instead of waiting for the second matching write. This weakens the hardening of the escalation-clear path and allows one faulty or glitched write to clear the class early.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when software writes one of the Alert Handler class clear CSRs while that register is still writable. The incorrect behavior is already visible on the first write itself; for example, the first write to the Class D clear CSR already generates the clear pulse that should only appear after a completed shadowed write sequence.

+## Errors, Faults and Alerts
 
-*  Software operation errors - These errors could have been caused by user errors and is a sign that software should examine its usage of key manager.
-   *  Invalid operation - An invalid operation (for example `generate` while in Reset) was invoked.

+The key manager has two overall categories of errors:
+* Recoverable errors
+* Fatal errors
 
-Two separate alerts are generated, one corresponding to each category above.
+Recoverable errors are those likely to have been introduced by software and not fatal to the key manager or the system.
+Fatal errors are logically impossible errors that have a high likelihood of being a fault and thus fatal.
+
+Each category of error can be further divided into two:
+* Synchronous errors
+* Asynchronous errors
+
+Synchronous errors happen only during a key manager transaction.
+Asynchronous errors can happen at any time.
+
+Given the above, we have 4 total categories of errors:
+* Synchronous recoverable errors
+* Asynchronous recoverable errors
+* Synchronous fatal errors
+* Asynchronous fatal errors
+
+All recoverable errors (synchronous and asynchronous) are captured in {{< regref ERR_CODE >}}.
+All fatal errors (synchronous and asynchronous) are captured in {{< regref FAULT_STATUS >}}.
+
+Recoverable errors cause a recoverable alert to be sent from the key manager.
+Fatal errors cause a fatal alert to be sent from the key manager.
+
+Below, the behavior of each category and its constituent errors are described in detail.
+
+### Synchronous Recoverable Errors
+
+These errors can only happen when a key manager transaction is invoked and are typically associated with incorrect software programming.
+At the end of the transaction, key manager reports whether there was an error in {{< regref ERR_CODE >}} and sends a recoverable alert.
+
+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.INVALID_OP >}} Software issued an invalid operation given the current key manager state.
+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.INVALID_KMAC_INPUT >}} Software supplied invalid input (for example a key greater than the max version) for a key manager operation.
+
+### Asynchronous Recoverable Errors
+
+These errors can happen at any time regardless of whether there is a key manager operation.
+The error is reported in {{< regref ERR_CODE >}} and the key manager sends a recoverable alert.
+
+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.INVALID_SHADOW_UPDATE >}} Software performed an invalid sequence while trying to update a key manager shadow register.
+
+### Synchronous Fatal Errors
+
+These errors can only happen when a key manager transaction is invoked and receives malformed transaction results that are not logically possible.
+At the end of the transaction, key manager reports whether there was an error in {{< regref FAULT_STATUS >}} and continuously sends fatal alerts .

+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.KMAC_OUT >}} KMAC returns all 0's or all 1's as a result, this is not possible given current definitions.
+
+Note, these errors are synchronous from the perspective of the key manager, but they may be asynchronous from the perspective of another module.
+
+### Asynchronous Fatal Errors
+
+These errors can happen at any time regardless of whether there is a key manager operation.
+The error is reported in {{< regref FAULT_STATUS >}} and the key manager continuously sends fatal alerts.

+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.KMAC_FSM >}} KMAC control's FSM is in an invalid state.
+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.REGFILE_INTG >}} The key manager's regfile reports an integrity error.
+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.SHADOW >}} The key manager's regfile reports a shadow storage error.
+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.CTRL_FSM_INTG >}} The key manager's main control FSM is in an invalid state.
+* {{< regref ERR_CODE.CTRL_FSM_CNT >}} The key manager's main control count exhibits an incorrect value.

problem_statement:
## Description
The affected module is the OpenTitan key manager (`keymgr`) control and fault-capture path for KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) digest responses. During key manager operations that wait for a KMAC digest, the returned masked digest shares are checked for invalid values.

## Expected Behavior
If the KMAC response for an in-flight key manager operation contains an invalid digest that should be classified as `FAULT_STATUS.KMAC_OUT` — for example, one returned digest share is all 0s or all 1s — the key manager must attribute that fault to the same operation. That operation must complete as a failure, not as a success, and software must be able to observe the `KMAC_OUT` fault for that transaction.

## Actual Behavior
When the invalid KMAC digest becomes visible only as the KMAC transaction is completing, the key manager can miss the `KMAC_OUT` fault. In that case, the operation completion is reported without the expected fault record, so software may observe a successful completion even though the returned digest was invalid.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when a key manager operation that uses KMAC reaches the end of the KMAC response and one of the returned masked digest shares is all 0s or all 1s.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's key manager (`keymgr`) is controlled by the life cycle controller. When software issues an `Advance` command while `keymgr` is in the `Reset` working state, `keymgr` begins the initialization sequence that moves it toward the `Initialized` state.

## Expected Behavior
If the life cycle controller disables `keymgr` before that initialization sequence finishes, the in-progress reset `Advance` must not be reported as a successful initialization. Instead, `keymgr` must take its wipe / invalid-operation handling path, and the operation must complete with `OP_STATUS` indicating failure and `ERR_CODE.INVALID_OP` set.

## Actual Behavior
If the life cycle controller disables `keymgr` during the reset `Advance` sequence, `keymgr` can still complete initialization as though it succeeded instead of terminating the operation as an invalid one.

## Affected Function
This affects the `keymgr` control logic for the `Reset`-to-`Initialized` initialization path, specifically its handling of a life cycle disable while an `Advance` from `Reset` is still in progress.

## Trigger Condition
Start an `Advance` operation from the `Reset` state, then have the life cycle controller disable `keymgr` before initialization reaches the `Initialized` state.

resolved_issues.title: [prim_esc_receiver] reserve ping corner case
resolved_issues.body:
Hi Michael,

I wonder if there is a corner case where the reverse ping might not work:

Here is the sequence I was thinking:
1). TB force esc_tx.esc_n to always be 1 to create a signal integrity error.
2). Send first ping request (that can trigger prim_esc_receiver's counters).
3). Ping request failed because esc_tx.esc_n is set to 1. -> However, it does not trigger an `ping_en` in prim_esc_receiver because of the signal integrity error, and ping counter never starts.
4). prim_esc_sender get the ping's signal integrity error, and triggers a real escalation request.
5). The escalation request always experiences signal integrity error because esc_tx.esc_n stays 1, and `esc_en_o` is not set in the `prim_esc_receiver`. So I think the escalation signal will never reach to the escalation receiver side.

Do you think we shall fix this?

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11466553/127077185-6ff6b66a-07ee-4fdc-b494-e936f015f4fe.png)

Thanks,
Cindy

resolved_issues.title: [alert] Candidates for hardening
resolved_issues.body:
A couple of things to look into and see if it is worth hardening

- the "[clear](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/alert_handler/rtl/alert_handler_esc_timer.sv#L160)" signal right now is not shadowed, which means it could potentially be glitched to skip all the escalation responses.  (@msfschaffner let me know if i misunderstood).

- when in "[terminal](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/alert_handler/rtl/alert_handler_esc_timer.sv#L261)" state all the escalation requests are turned off. Does it make sense when in terminal to just fire all escalations? This is not really that important since the liklihood of glitching into `Terminal` is low due to sparse encoding and redundant counters.

- Question - when escalation sender observes an [error](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/prim/rtl/prim_esc_sender.sv#L199) does it make sense to cycle back to idle, or should we progress to a state that would both request escalation forever and timeout on pings? The error observed might be a result of a glitch between escalation sender / receiver.  This is closely related to the alert clock/power boundary discussion.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's `prim_esc_receiver` primitive decodes a differential escalation input from `prim_esc_sender` and also participates in the ping mechanism that checks whether the escalation channel is intact. The affected behavior is the receiver-side local escalation output (`esc_en_o` in the buggy implementation).

## Expected Behavior
If the incoming differential escalation pair `esc_tx_i.esc_p` / `esc_tx_i.esc_n` becomes invalid, the receiver must enter local escalation and assert its local escalation output instead of only reporting an integrity error on the response path back to the sender. This also applies to the corner case where the fault is first encountered during a ping used to verify the escalation channel and the sender subsequently treats the failed ping as an escalation condition: the receiver must still assert its local escalation output rather than drop the escalation on the receiver side.

## Actual Behavior
`prim_esc_receiver` detects the invalid same-level differential input and reports the integrity problem on its response path, but it does not assert the local escalation output. As a result, escalation can be lost at the receiver side even though the channel has already been identified as corrupted. In the ping corner case, a ping can fail because of the corrupted input pair and the receiver still does not raise its local escalation output.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when the `prim_esc_receiver` input differential pair `esc_tx_i.esc_p/n` is driven into an invalid same-level state, for example because one side is stuck and both wires match, during either a direct escalation request or a ping transaction.

## Implementation Constraint
The local escalation output of the affected escalation receiver path should use the exact token `esc_req_o` rather than `esc_en_o`, while still representing the receiver's local escalation request behavior.

title: [sw/silicon_creator] Use OTP library in shutdown module
body:
[sw/silicon_creator] Use OTP library in shutdown module
1. Follow the redaction policy in #7353 (no redaction in RMA and
   test unlocked lifecycle states).
2. Use the OTP library to read from OTP.

The OTP and lifecycle libraries use sec_mmio underneath the hood.
Since sec_mmio can trigger a call to shutdown_finalize we need to
avoid calling it from shutdown_finalize. To acheive this a new
shutdown_redact_policy function has been added that determines
the redaction policy to apply without using either library.

1. Follow the redaction policy in #7353 (no redaction in RMA and

2. Use the OTP library to read from OTP.

The OTP and lifecycle libraries use sec_mmio underneath the hood.
Since sec_mmio can trigger a call to shutdown_finalize we need to
avoid calling it from shutdown_finalize. To acheive this a new
shutdown_redact_policy function has been added that determines
the redaction policy to apply without using either library.

This change required an increase in the number of registers that

resolved_issues.title: [sw/silicon_creator] sigverify related OTP values during manufacturing
resolved_issues.body:
#7306 and #7351 adds OTP support for
* checking the validity of public keys and 
* determining which mod_exp implementation (sw or otbn) should be used

assuming that these OTP items have already been programmed. Since we need to run ROM_EXT images before these items are programmed during manufacturing, `sigverify.c` and `sigverify_keys.c` should be updated so that
* all keys are considered valid, and
* software mod_exp implementation is used

during manufacturing (at least until the relevant OTP items are programmed).

We discussed this briefly with @moidx offline and came up with the following options:

| Option | Value(s) interpreted as `false` | Value(s) interpreted as `true` | Invalid values |
|-|-|-|-|
|1 (Use OTP only for disabling) | A falsy value | All other values | None |
|2 (Allow default values) | A falsy value | A truthy value and the _default_ OTP value  | All other values
|3 (Allow default values only in certain lifecycle states) | A falsy value  | A truthy value and the _default_ OTP value **only** in certain LC states | All other values |
|4 (Do not read OTP in certain LC states, just assume defaults) | A falsy value | A truthy value  | All other values |

(E.g., falsy value: `kHardenedBoolFalse`, truthy value: `kHardenedBoolTrue`, default value: all `0`s)

I'm leaning towards the 3rd or the 4th options above and would like to hear your thoughts @moidx @cfrantz. Also, should we allow default values in all test LC states or should we be more granular?

problem_statement:
The affected component is the Mask ROM shutdown finalization path in OpenTitan's silicon_creator subsystem. During fatal shutdown, this path reports a ROM error code and may redact parts of that code based on the chip lifecycle state and an OTP (One-Time Programmable) setting that controls ROM error reporting.

Expected behavior: if shutdown is entered while the chip is in the RMA (Return Material Authorization) lifecycle state, the reported error code must not be redacted. Even when the OTP error-reporting setting requests module redaction, `shutdown_finalize()` should emit the original full ROM error value.

Actual behavior: the current shutdown reporting path still follows the OTP redaction setting in RMA. When module redaction is configured, the reported shutdown error loses its module information instead of remaining fully visible.

Trigger condition: invoke `shutdown_finalize()` with a nonzero ROM error while the lifecycle state is RMA and the OTP error-reporting policy is set to redact the module portion of the error code.

resolved_issues.title: [rtl/rstmgr] Disable alert and cpu capture for low power exit
resolved_issues.body:
Cpu and alert info is captured on resets in order to provide additional details regarding the reset cause. When such capture happens the hardware disables subsequent captures until software re-enables it writing into the `cpu_info_ctrl.en` and `alert_info_ctrl.en` CSR fields.

Capture is also triggered by resets due to a low power exit, even though this is not a reset that will need diagnostics. This is problematic since it is possible a low power exit reset is closely followed in time by some hardware triggered exit if software has had no time to re-enable captures. This would mean the latter reset would not capture information, and instead the captured info would correspond to the uninteresting low power exit reset.

This can be resolved easily by dropping the low power exit from the causes of reset capture... it even reduces the logic.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's reset manager (`rstmgr`) stores alert and CPU crash-dump information in the `alert_info` and `cpu_info` control/status registers (CSRs) when capture is enabled through the `alert_info_ctrl.en` and `cpu_info_ctrl.en` bits. These enable bits are intended to act like a one-shot arm for reset-driven diagnostic capture.

## Expected Behavior
If alert and CPU crash-dump capture is enabled and the chip takes either a reset caused by low-power exit or a non-debug-module (NDM) reset, `reset_info` should report that reset cause, the captured `alert_info` and `cpu_info` contents should reflect the sampled dump values for that reset, and both enable bits should remain set after the reset. A hardware reset request is the reset cause that should consume the one-shot arm: after a hardware-reset capture, `alert_info_ctrl.en` and `cpu_info_ctrl.en` should clear until software re-enables them.

## Actual Behavior
The implementation clears `alert_info_ctrl.en` and `cpu_info_ctrl.en` after any crash-info capture, including captures triggered by low-power-exit resets and NDM resets. That makes those resets consume the one-shot arm, so later resets cannot capture new alert or CPU crash information until software rewrites the enable bits.

## Affected Module
This bug is in the reset manager (`rstmgr`) alert and CPU crash-dump capture control, specifically the logic that decides when `alert_info_ctrl.en` and `cpu_info_ctrl.en` are cleared.

## Trigger Condition
Enable alert and CPU crash-dump capture, then trigger either a low-power-exit reset or an NDM reset. After that reset completes, the bug appears if `alert_info_ctrl.en` and `cpu_info_ctrl.en` have been cleared instead of remaining enabled.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan Alert Handler IP can update its crashdump output (`crashdump_o`) when an alert class reaches a configured escalation phase. The `crashdump_trigger_shadowed` configuration selects that phase; a value of `0` means the crashdump should be captured for Phase0.

## Expected Behavior
When crashdump capture is configured for Phase0, starting escalation should update `crashdump_o` only after the reported class escalation state has become `Phase0`. The captured status for that event must not still show the previous `Idle` state.

## Actual Behavior
The crashdump update can occur one clock cycle too early. With `crashdump_trigger_shadowed = 0`, `crashdump_o` may be captured while the reported class escalation state is still `Idle`, so the crashdump status reflects the pre-escalation state instead of `Phase0`.

## Affected Function
This affects the Alert Handler IP's crashdump capture behavior for escalation-state reporting.

## Trigger Condition
The issue is triggered when an alert class begins escalation while crashdump capture is configured for Phase0 (`crashdump_trigger_shadowed = 0`). In that situation, the crashdump can be updated on the same transition into Phase0, before Phase0 is visible in the reported escalation state.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan flash controller contains a life cycle manager submodule, `flash_ctrl_lcmgr`, that sequences the Return Material Authorization (RMA) flash wipe flow. In the affected implementation, the RMA transition finite-state machine (FSM) is encoded in a way that allows a single-bit state upset to turn one valid RMA state into another valid RMA state, so the corruption can be mistaken for a legal transition.

## Expected Behavior
Any single-bit corruption of the stored RMA transition state must be treated as a fatal life cycle manager fault. The module must not accept the corrupted encoding as a valid next RMA step, and it must assert the life cycle manager's fatal error indication instead of remaining in its normal no-error state.

## Actual Behavior
With the legacy RMA FSM encoding, a one-bit upset can move the FSM from one legal state encoding to another. When that happens, `flash_ctrl_lcmgr` continues as if the new state were valid, so the state corruption is not detected as fatal.

## Affected Function
The bug affects the OpenTitan flash controller's life cycle manager submodule, `flash_ctrl_lcmgr`, specifically the RMA transition FSM that controls the secure wipe sequence.

## Trigger Conditions
The bug is triggered by a transient single-bit upset in the stored RMA FSM state. A representative boundary case is an upset while the module is idle before RMA processing starts: the idle-state encoding flips to a different valid RMA state encoding, and the module does not report the corruption as a fatal error.
