problem_statement:
## Description
The SPI Device IP's flash-mode 4-byte address-configuration logic can lose a newly applied address-mode command when two SPI transactions are separated by little or no chip-select-bar (CSB) inactive time. In this context, EN4B enters 4-byte address mode and EX4B exits 4-byte address mode. The failure occurs in the path that keeps the flash-mode 4-byte address setting aligned between the SPI-clock-domain state and the software-visible configuration bit.

## Expected Behavior
After the SPI Device accepts EN4B, 4-byte address mode must remain enabled until a later EX4B command changes it. After the SPI Device accepts EX4B, 4-byte address mode must remain disabled until a later EN4B command changes it. A follow-up SPI transaction that is not another address-mode command, including a back-to-back status read, must not restore the previous address-width setting. Once synchronization completes, the software-readable `cfg.addr_4b_en` bit must report the same stable mode.

## Actual Behavior
If EN4B or EX4B is followed too quickly by another SPI transaction, the next CSB assertion can reapply an older mirrored value before the new state has fully propagated. This makes the 4-byte address setting transient. For example, EX4B can clear 4-byte mode briefly and then the mode becomes enabled again on the following transaction even though no new EN4B command was received.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered in SPI Device flash mode when EN4B or EX4B is immediately followed by another SPI transaction with very short or zero CSB inactive time. A concrete manifestation is an EN4B or EX4B command followed right away by a status-read transaction; repeated alternation between EN4B and EX4B under this short-idle condition exposes the stale-state overwrite.

body:
Fixes #15257

Specifically this follows the "Focussed RTL solution" in that issue.

This commit creates a 2-bit shift register that gets set when a SHA corruption event is detected.  This shift register is used to drop the following two SHA outputs after the corruption event. Once those two outputs have been dropped the shift register is clear and further outputs are accepted.

resolved_issues.title: [entropy_src] Scoreboarding mispredicts SHA output in rare exception case
resolved_issues.body:
This issue describes an `entropy_src_fw_ov` test failure that is likely rare and really only appears when the test (intentionally) violates the `entropy_src` usage model.

When in "entropy_insert" mode the `entropy_src` programming model requires that the application check `fw_ov_wr_fifo_full` register before deasserting `fw_ov_sha3_start`.  This prevents the initiation of SHA3 processing while the last inserted word is still in the pipeline, but not yet added to the SHA3 message.  Failure to do this check triggers an recoverable alert, and the output of the SHA3 conditioner is technically undefined,    

The last inserted word usually remains in the pipeline, outside the SHA3 engine.  In this case both the current and the following digest will be altered. (The current digest will be missing an input, and the following digest will have an extra input).   However the backpressure can clear before the SHA engine actually starts processing, in which case the usage model violation does not have any negative effects.

However scoreboarding currently attempts to keep the simulation running by assuming that the SHA3 outputs are briefly corrupted, by the misplacement of the input data. (Short of monitoring more internal signals such as SHA3 ports, or the `main_sm` state, there is no way to detect whether corruption actually occurs).   This however leads to test failures in cases when where the usage violation causes no corruption.

In such cases the DUT is behaving exactly as currently specified: an alert is logged, yet the output is corrupted (with as much as 64 less bits of entropy in the first output, and up to 64 extra bits of entropy in the following output).  There are two ways to handle this.
1.)  If this behavior is deemed acceptable, then a DV fix is in order to simply note that the corrupted outputs may be mispredicted. 
2.)  One could also make an RTL fix to suppress the output of corrupted words.  DV would then only need to note the corruption and anticipate that the output is discarded.

The priority of this fix probably depends on the desired course of action.  If it is deemed that an fix is required for this firmware exception case it should probably be labeled as P1, however if only a DV fix is required this rare care (at most once in 50 runs) likely will not impact nightly regressions much and can be treated as P2.

Labelling this issue as P1 until a course of action is decided.

problem_statement:
## Description
The Entropy Source (`entropy_src`) IP mishandles a firmware-override exception in its SHA3 conditioning path. In `entropy_insert` mode, software can inject words that are collected and processed by the SHA3 conditioner before a seed is sent to the final seed path. Software is required to keep `fw_ov_sha3_start` asserted until `fw_ov_wr_fifo_full` indicates that the last injected word has drained out of the write-side buffer and into the SHA3 input path. If software deasserts `fw_ov_sha3_start` too early, one injected word may still be in flight, which raises a recoverable alert and makes the next SHA3-conditioned outputs ambiguous.

## Expected Behavior
When that recoverable-alert condition occurs while the SHA3 conditioning path is active (that is, not in bypass mode), the `entropy_src` core must conservatively suppress the next two SHA3-conditioned outputs from being pushed into the final seed FIFO. This requirement applies even in the rare case where backpressure clears quickly enough that those outputs would have been valid, because the hardware cannot reliably distinguish that case from a genuinely corrupted digest. After those two candidate outputs are discarded, later SHA3-conditioned outputs should be forwarded normally.

## Actual Behavior
The recoverable alert is recorded, but the `entropy_src` core can still forward the next two SHA3-conditioned outputs into the final seed FIFO. In the common corruption case, the digest currently being completed can be missing one 64-bit input word and the following digest can incorrectly include that stray word, yet both outputs may still be treated as valid and forwarded.

## Affected Function
This affects the `entropy_src` core's firmware-override SHA3 conditioner output gating, specifically the logic that decides whether SHA3-conditioned outputs are allowed to enter the final seed FIFO after this firmware-override disable error.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered in firmware override `entropy_insert` mode when the SHA3 conditioning path is enabled instead of bypass mode, and software deasserts `fw_ov_sha3_start` before `fw_ov_wr_fifo_full` indicates that the last injected word has drained into the SHA3 input path. Once that recoverable-alert condition occurs, the next two candidate SHA3-conditioned outputs are the outputs that must be suppressed.

problem_statement:
## Description
The Reset Manager (RSTMGR) exposes an `ERR_CODE` status register that records internal faults. One of its bits, `ERR_CODE.fsm_err`, is set when RSTMGR detects a finite-state machine (FSM) error such as an invalid FSM state.

## Expected Behavior
When hardware asserts `ERR_CODE.fsm_err`, a concurrent software access to `ERR_CODE` must not clear that newly reported fault. After the concurrent hardware update and software transaction complete, `ERR_CODE.fsm_err` must still read back as `1` so software can observe the error.

## Actual Behavior
Because `ERR_CODE` is implemented as a write-one-to-clear (RW1C) register, software can write `1` to `ERR_CODE` at the same time that hardware raises `fsm_err`. In that corner case, the newly detected FSM error can be cleared immediately, so `ERR_CODE.fsm_err` reads back as `0` even though the fault was just reported.

## Affected Function
This bug affects the Reset Manager (RSTMGR) CSR block, specifically the `ERR_CODE` register's `fsm_err` bit and the path that reports internal FSM faults into that register.

## Trigger Condition
The failure occurs when software writes to `ERR_CODE` while RSTMGR hardware asserts `ERR_CODE.fsm_err`, for example when an invalid FSM state is detected at the same time that software writes `1` to the `fsm_err` bit.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan key manager (keymgr) has a sideload key controller that delivers hardware-generated keys directly to AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code), or OTBN (OpenTitan Big Number Accelerator). Its `KEYMGR.SIDE_LOAD_SEL.CTRL.CONSISTENCY` protection does not reliably detect when the sideload key slot for an unselected destination becomes valid during a sideload key generation operation.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the key manager sideload path, specifically the destination-consistency check for the AES, KMAC, and OTBN sideload key slots.

## Expected Behavior
During a hardware-output (sideload) key generation operation, only the sideload slot for the selected destination may assert `valid`. If any other destination's sideload slot asserts `valid` while the operation is in progress, the key manager must report a side-load selection consistency fault for that operation.

## Actual Behavior
The current implementation can miss this condition, so an unselected destination's sideload slot may assert `valid` without the key manager reporting the corresponding side-load selection fault.

## Trigger Conditions
This is triggered during a sideload key generation operation when the command targets one hardware consumer, but the sideload slot for a different consumer asserts `valid` before the operation completes.

problem_statement:
## Description
In OpenTitan's power manager (pwrmgr), the fast power-state finite-state machine (FSM) keeps track of whether the boot straps have already been sampled during startup. A non-debug-module (NDM) reset can occur after the device has already completed its initial boot sequence, and that reset path should not be treated as a fresh boot for strap sampling.

## Expected Behavior
After a power-on reset (POR) or hardware reset, the pwrmgr fast FSM may issue one strap-sampling request during startup. Once startup has completed and the straps have been sampled, a later NDM reset must preserve that sampled state. When the system comes back from an NDM reset, the FSM must return to active operation without issuing a second strap-sampling request. Re-sampling is only correct for reset types that represent a fresh boot, such as POR or hardware reset.

## Actual Behavior
In the current implementation, if the device boots, performs its initial strap sample, and later receives an NDM reset, the pwrmgr startup flow behaves as though the straps were never sampled. On the restart after the NDM reset, the FSM issues another strap-sampling request, so the straps are sampled a second time even though there was no POR or hardware reset.

## Affected Function
The bug is in the pwrmgr fast power-state FSM logic that tracks the `strap_sampled` state and decides whether to emit the strap-sampling request during startup.

## Trigger Condition
Trigger the bug by completing a normal boot sequence with one strap sample, then asserting an NDM reset. When the system restarts from that NDM reset, the design incorrectly performs strap sampling again instead of preserving the existing sampled state.

problem_statement:
## Description
The affected module is the OpenTitan key manager's sideload-key controller finite state machine (FSM), `keymgr_sideload_key_ctrl`. This submodule manages hardware-only sideload keys that are delivered directly to hardware consumers instead of software-readable outputs. The design marks this controller with the `SIDELOAD_CTRL.FSM.SPARSE` security countermeasure, meaning invalid state encodings should be detectable as sideload-controller FSM integrity faults, but the sideload controller state storage is not actually covered by that sparse-FSM protection.

## Expected Behavior
After the key manager has been initialized and advanced out of reset into normal operation, corruption of the sideload controller FSM state storage must be detected as an asynchronous fatal fault. The key manager must raise the `fatal_fault_err` alert, set `FAULT_STATUS.SIDE_CTRL_FSM`, move `working_state` to `Invalid`, and any subsequent key-manager operation must complete with failure.

## Actual Behavior
The sideload controller FSM is missing the intended sparse-FSM integrity coverage. As a result, the sideload controller state register is not handled through the expected `SIDE_CTRL_FSM` integrity-fault path for this submodule.

## Trigger Condition
The problem is exposed after initialization, once the key manager has already advanced into a normal idle or operational state and no new operation is currently in progress. If the sideload controller FSM state register is corrupted in that condition, the design does not report the expected sideload-controller FSM integrity fault behavior.

From what I see in the waves:
1). https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/edn/rtl/edn_core.sv#L592
`auto_req_mode_busy` is reset to 0 when there is no valid TL transaction to `sw_gen_cmd` register.
(In tl DV agent, we will drive "X" data when there is no valid transaction)

2). Tracing back, looks like 
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/edn/rtl/edn_main_sm.sv#L255
`auto_req_mode_busy_o` is only set to 1 when edn_enable_i = 1, otherwise it uses the default value 0.

3). So right after the EDN disablement happens, gencmd_fifo streamed in "X" data.

I will try to clean up and push a draft PR so you can reproduce it on your end :)

Cindy

problem_statement:
## Description
The bug is in the Entropy Distribution Network (EDN) core's automatic-request generate-command path, specifically the logic that feeds the internal generate-command FIFO (`gencmd_fifo`) while EDN is issuing a generate command to the Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generator (CSRNG).

## Expected Behavior
If EDN is disabled during this automatic-request flow, the disable transition must not cause `gencmd_fifo` to accept a command word containing unknown (`X`) bits. After disable, either no additional word should be pushed into `gencmd_fifo`, or any pushed word must be fully defined.

## Actual Behavior
When software disables EDN during `AutoSendGenCmd`, `gencmd_fifo` can still receive one more entry, and that entry can contain unknown (`X`) data instead of a defined generate command word.

## Trigger Conditions
This occurs when software disables EDN while automatic request mode is in `AutoSendGenCmd`, the state used to send a generate command. At that disable boundary, `gencmd_fifo` can still be written even though the command value is no longer guaranteed to be defined.

problem_statement:
## Description
The HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) hardware IP block in OpenTitan exposes a single alert output. At the top-level system integration, that alert is treated as a fatal alert source, but the HMAC alert sender does not classify its only alert as fatal. As a result, the HMAC alert behaves like a recoverable alert even though the rest of the system expects fatal-alert behavior.

## Expected Behavior
HMAC's single alert output must use fatal-alert semantics. After an HMAC alert has been observed, acknowledging the corresponding alert cause while the HMAC clock is gated off must not permanently retire the condition. When the HMAC clock is enabled again, the OpenTitan alert handler should observe the HMAC alert cause asserted again.

## Actual Behavior
The initial HMAC alert can be observed, but if the HMAC clock is disabled before the alert cause is acknowledged, the cause clears on acknowledge and remains cleared after the clock is restored. This is recoverable-alert behavior, not fatal-alert behavior.

## Affected Module
The bug is in the HMAC IP's single alert output path, specifically the severity classification passed to the alert sender that reports HMAC faults to the OpenTitan alert handler.

## Trigger Conditions
The issue appears when an HMAC alert is triggered, the HMAC peripheral clock is turned off during alert handling, the alert cause is acknowledged while that clock is off, and the clock is later turned back on.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan Key Manager (keymgr) IP mishandles its life cycle (LC) enable input during the reset-to-initialization path. If the life cycle controller deasserts `keymgr_en` during the first `advance` operation after reset, keymgr can still complete that command as if it succeeded even though LC disable should invalidate the block and wipe its secrets.

## Expected Behavior
If the life cycle controller disables keymgr before initialization has completed, keymgr must not continue into an initialized working state. The in-flight first `advance` operation must be reported as a failed or invalid operation rather than a success, and the block must end in the `Invalid` working state.

## Actual Behavior
When `keymgr_en` is deasserted during the first `advance` after reset, keymgr may report successful completion. After that, it wipes keys and moves to the `Invalid` state, so the externally visible status of the command is inconsistent with the fact that keymgr was disabled.

## Affected Function
This affects the Key Manager (keymgr) control logic that consumes the life cycle controller's `keymgr_en` signal during initialization and updates the working state and operation status for the first `advance` after reset.

## Trigger Condition
Start the first `advance` used to bring keymgr out of reset, then deassert the life cycle controller's `keymgr_en` signal before initialization finishes.

problem_statement:
## Description
In the Entropy Distribution Network (EDN) IP, the fatal error reporting interface is inconsistent for the output first-in, first-out (FIFO) path. The issue report notes that the `ERR_CODE` register describes bits `[19:2]` as reserved, but writing value `2` to `ERR_CODE_TEST` can still trigger a fatal alert. Bit 2 is associated with the output FIFO error source, so the software-visible status map does not match the error-injection map.

## Expected Behavior
`ERR_CODE_TEST` and `ERR_CODE` should use the same error-bit mapping. When software writes `2` to `ERR_CODE_TEST`, the EDN should report the corresponding fatal error source in `ERR_CODE[2]` instead of treating bit 2 as reserved. This makes the alert source identifiable to firmware.

## Actual Behavior
Writing `2` to `ERR_CODE_TEST` can trigger the fatal alert path, but `ERR_CODE[2]` is not exposed as a defined output FIFO error status bit. Software can therefore observe a fatal EDN failure without a matching `ERR_CODE` indication for that source.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is EDN fatal error status and error-injection handling for the output FIFO path, specifically the mapping between the `ERR_CODE_TEST` and `ERR_CODE` registers.

## Trigger Condition
The inconsistency is observable when software writes value `2` to the EDN `ERR_CODE_TEST` register to inject the output FIFO fatal error condition.

title: [aes] Improve FI detection when OR-combining multi-rail signals
body:
This is needed for #16427.

Previously, OR-combination and error detection for multi-bit, multi-rail signals was done in a single for loop inside an always_comb block. In every loop iteration, the current combined signal was only compared to the current signal added to the combination. This is not ideal from a fault detection perspective.

For example, when faulting the last rail of the round counter to 1 when the counter is actually 0 wouldn't be detected immediately. For the first and second loop iteration, the OR-combined value was still 0. For the last rail, the OR-combined value would be 1 which is equal to the faulted counter. In practice this didn't really matter because a faulted round counter itself isn't problematic. But the faulted round counter changes the control flow of one rail which is always detected, e.g., by a register write enable signal taking on an invalid encoding as the different rails driving that get out of sync.

This minimal RTL change performs the comparison in a separate loop to effectively compare all rails with the total OR-combined value. In the example above, the final OR-combined counter value is compared against both un-faulted rails and the fault is immediately detected.

The associated area impact of this change is neglibile. With Yosys + nangate45, AES is now 110.17 kGE vs. 109.86 kGE (+0.28%). But it improves FI detection and most importantly simplifies DV as faults in the round counter are detected immediately and independent whether the AES cipher core is busy or idle.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's AES IP uses redundant multi-rail control values as a fault-detection mechanism. In the AES cipher-control path, the redundant round counter is OR-combined across rails and then checked for consistency. With the current logic, a fault on the last rail can escape immediate detection: if that rail is corrupted from 0 to 1 while the cipher-control state machine is idle and the true round-counter value is 0, the mismatch is not reported when it occurs.

## Expected Behavior
Whenever the AES cipher-control logic evaluates the redundant round counter, every rail must agree with the final OR-combined counter value. If any rail disagrees, including while the cipher-control state machine is idle, the AES block must treat the condition as an internal fault and raise its fatal fault alert without waiting for later control-flow divergence or for a new AES round to begin.

## Actual Behavior
A mismatch on the last round-counter rail can be missed in the idle state. When that rail is faulted from 0 to 1 while the true counter value is 0, the AES block does not immediately raise its fatal fault alert at the point of corruption. The inconsistency may only become visible later after it perturbs downstream control behavior.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the AES IP's cipher-control round-counter redundancy check (`AES_CIPHER.CTR.REDUN`), specifically the consistency check for the OR-combined multi-rail round counter.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when the AES cipher-control state machine is idle, the redundant round counter's true value is 0, and the last rail of that multi-rail counter is corrupted from 0 to 1.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan I2C controller IP has a host-mode repeated-START timing bug. Software issues host transfers through the format FIFO (FMT FIFO), the queue used to send host-side transfer commands, and a repeated START is requested by queuing a new entry with the START flag while the current transaction is still active. In this situation, the host controller can leave the current SCL-low phase early and jump directly into repeated-START generation.

## Expected Behavior
When a repeated START is requested during an active host transaction, the controller must complete the current programmed SCL low phase before beginning the repeated-START sequence. The low pulse immediately before the repeated START must not be shorter than the configured low-period timing (`TIMING0.TLOW`); the controller should follow the normal clock sequence instead of truncating that pulse.

## Actual Behavior
Instead, the controller can cut the low SCL pulse short and begin the repeated START early. This changes the bus waveform seen by the target and can cause write-transaction mismatches in verification. In the failing regression that opened the issue, `TLOW` was programmed to `0xC`, but the low period before the repeated START lasted only 9 cycles.

## Affected Function
This affects the OpenTitan I2C IP host-mode controller state machine, specifically repeated-START handling for commands taken from the format FIFO (FMT FIFO).

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when software queues another START instead of a STOP while a host-mode transfer is already in progress, producing a repeated START between back-to-back transfers.

resolved_issues.body:
- [x] The attributes for hardware access to creator/owner seed pages is different from software access. This does not really make sense since if the two sides do not agree, the contents in there would always be non-sense. We should consider streamlining this #16799
- [ ] The info pages currently do not have a "Default" config the way data pages do.  This may not make sense and deserves a second look.
- [x] The status register does not indicate when flash is actually initialized, just whether its busy. This means it is possible for software to interpret something that has never initialized with something that has finished initializing.  #16795

from pathlib import Path

root = Path("/home/opentitan")

seq = root / "hw/ip/flash_ctrl/dv/env/seq_lib/flash_ctrl_init_status_vseq.sv"
seq.write_text(
    """// Copyright lowRISC contributors.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

class flash_ctrl_init_status_vseq extends flash_ctrl_base_vseq;
  `uvm_object_utils(flash_ctrl_init_status_vseq)
  `uvm_object_new

    uvm_reg_data_t status;

    csr_rd(.ptr(ral.status), .value(status));
    initialized = (status >> 5) & 1'b1;

    `uvm_info(`gfn, $sformatf("flash status after init: 0x%0h", status), UVM_MEDIUM)
    if (status[4]) begin
      `uvm_fatal(`gfn, $sformatf("init_wip should be 0 after initialization, got status=0x%0h",
                                 status))
    end
    if (!initialized) begin
      `uvm_fatal(`gfn, $sformatf("initialized bit should be 1 after initialization, got status=0x%0h",
                                 status))
    end
  endtask : body
endclass : flash_ctrl_init_status_vseq
"""
)

def insert_once(path: Path, anchor: str, addition: str) -> None:
    text = path.read_text()
    if addition in text:
        return
    if anchor not in text:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Anchor not found in {path}: {anchor}")
    path.write_text(text.replace(anchor, anchor + addition, 1))

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan flash controller (`flash_ctrl`) `STATUS` Control and Status Register (CSR) indicates whether flash initialization is busy, but it does not indicate whether flash initialization has completed. This makes it possible for software to confuse a controller that has finished initializing and is now idle with a controller that has not initialized at all.

## Expected Behavior
Once flash initialization completes, the `STATUS` CSR must let firmware distinguish two states: "initialization still in progress" and "initialization completed." In particular, when initialization has finished and the controller is idle, the status must show both that initialization is no longer busy and that initialization has completed.

## Actual Behavior
The current `STATUS` CSR only reports whether initialization is busy. After the busy indication clears, software cannot tell whether initialization completed successfully or whether the controller is simply not initialized, because both cases appear as not busy.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the flash controller (`flash_ctrl`) software-visible initialization status reporting through the `STATUS` CSR.

## Trigger Condition
This bug is exposed when firmware polls the flash controller `STATUS` CSR as the controller transitions from initialization-in-progress to the idle post-initialization state.

title: [spid] Passthrough to support CPOL 1
body:
_Related Issue: https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/16339 _

Previously, passthrough logic had a bug when CPOL is 1. When SCK is inverted, meaning that the SCK remains high when CSb is de-asserted, the filtering logic did not behave correctly.

The reason is the clock gating cell. To filter out the current command, passthrough logic gates the output clock then delays the CSb and release the CSb. The clock enable signal drops when the command needs to be filtered. The logic sets the enable signal when CSb is released.

However, if CPOL is 1, then setting the enable signal enables the SCK at the next low period of SCK, which is the beginning of the next transaction. So, the next transaction misses one clock edge.

This commit tries to address the issue by:

1. Adding inverter in front of/ and at the end of the CG cell
2. Adding a CG for inverted clock.
3. Adding a MUX between normal SCK and inverted SCK selected by CPOL

This solution adds 2x inverter and one AND delay onto the SCK path.

resolved_issues.title: [spi_device] SPI pass-through does not support mode 3
resolved_issues.body:
**TLDR;** SCK doesn't return to idle for filtered commands in mode 3

>SPI mode 3: CPOL=1, CPHA=1, DataOut=SCLK-falling-edge, DataIn=SCLK-rising-edge

I found we didn't set phase/polarity correctly in the device side of the SPI agent. When I tried to fix it, this issue came up.

In this waveform, the first sck is driven by host. The 2nd sck is what downstream sees. The `en_latch` is set too late and downstream misses the first falling edge of sck.
The `en_latch` is affected by the previous command, depending on whether is filtered.
![Screen Shot 2022-11-14 at 2 59 46 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/49293026/201786086-03fbb438-bc81-468f-8abf-95b3a27dca89.png)

It will be good to test the spi_device with a real flash model on the downstream port, which ensures our design compliant with the SPI flash protocol. Maybe we can do this in V3.

Command to open the waveform session:

> cd /mnt/disks/filestores/opentitan-shared/users/weicai/scratch/new1/spi_device-sim-vcs/0.spi_device_flash_all/latest; verdi -ssr Verdi.ses &

problem_statement:
## Description
The SPI Device (`spi_device`) IP's flash passthrough path does not correctly handle SPI mode 3 traffic when command filtering blocks one transaction and the next transaction is forwarded. In SPI mode 3, clock polarity (CPOL) = 1 and clock phase (CPHA) = 1, so the serial clock (SCK) is expected to idle high while chip select (CSb, active low) is de-asserted. After a filtered command, the downstream flash-facing SCK can be re-enabled too late at the transaction boundary.

## Expected Behavior
In flash passthrough mode, command filtering must not change the clock behavior seen by the downstream flash on the next forwarded transaction. After a command is filtered while CPOL = 1, the downstream SCK must return to its idle-high level while CSb is de-asserted, and the following forwarded transaction must present the complete mode-3 clock sequence, including its first falling edge.

## Actual Behavior
When a filtered command is immediately followed by a forwarded command in flash passthrough mode with CPOL = 1 and CPHA = 1, the downstream device can miss the first falling edge of SCK. This means the forwarded transaction no longer matches a valid SPI mode 3 waveform and the downstream flash can sample command or data bits at the wrong time.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the SPI Device (`spi_device`) IP's flash passthrough path, specifically the interaction between command filtering and downstream SCK generation toward the attached flash device.

## Trigger Condition
This bug is triggered when an upstream SPI host/master uses flash passthrough mode in SPI mode 3, the command filter blocks one transaction, and the next transaction is allowed through to the downstream flash.

title: [flash_ctrl] Fix buffer enable / disable timing
body:
- fixes #16979
- In the previou design, the buffer enable was allowed to change whenever the read pipeline was idle.  This however does not account for the scenario where on the same cycle there is a new flash read request.  In the buffer enable were changed from 1->0, it would allow a new request to match a buffer entry, while disallowing that buffer from responding in subsequent cycles.
- Update the design such that when buffer enable is changed the request is back pressured during that same cycle.

Signed-off-by: Timothy Chen <timothytim@google.com>

problem_statement:
## Description
The bug affects the OpenTitan flash controller (`flash_ctrl`) during the handoff between a controller-initiated flash read and a life cycle RMA (Return Merchandise Authorization) request. If an RMA request arrives while a controller read is still active, the controller read path can fail to retire cleanly and block forward progress of the RMA sequence.

## Trigger Condition
A controller-initiated flash read is already in progress, and an RMA request is asserted before that read operation has completed.

## Expected Behavior
When an RMA request is issued during an active controller read, the flash controller must allow the in-flight read to complete, and the RMA flow must advance into its erase phase without hanging.

## Actual Behavior
In the failing scenario, issuing an RMA request during a controller read leaves the controller read path stuck. The controller read does not complete, and the RMA sequence fails to advance into its erase phase, so the operation times out.

title: [sram_ctrl] Fix RMW corner case when escalating
body:
If a global escalation request and a RMW transaction come in at the same time, the RMW transaction will not be able to complete even though the TL gate allows for transactions that are already pending inside the device to respond back (to make the bus behavior less erratic for a better SW debug experience).

The reason for this is the write part of the RMW transaction, since the scrambling device blocks any transaction in case the keys have been invalidated due to escalation.

This patch fixes this corner case by specifically allowing pending writes to complete upon escalation.

The rationale is that a write won't give an attacker any advantage, especially since the scrambling keys are already clobbered at that point, and the TL gate is not accepting any additional transactions from the bus.

Fixes #17064.

Signed-off-by: Michael Schaffner <msf@google.com>

repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

I tried to hit the condition (outstanding_txn != 0), as it was shown uncovered.

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace (+submodules)
cd /home/opentitan
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx
git checkout d08cfa77da7116c03c3a9dd085023cbe5e48f3ae
git submodule update --init --recursive

# Stage 2: install repository apt dependencies (if present)
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
if [[ -f apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing apt dependencies from apt-requirements.txt"
  cp apt-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  sed -i -e '/^$/d' -e '/^#/d' -e 's/#.*//' /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  if [[ -s /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
    apt-get update
    xargs -r apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends < /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  else
    echo "[INFO] apt-requirements.txt is empty after filtering comments"
  fi
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[WARN] apt-requirements.txt not found at d08cfa77da7116c03c3a9dd085023cbe5e48f3ae; skipping repo-specific apt install"
fi

# Stage 3: install project-specific Python dependencies from the checked-out repo
if [[ -f python-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Python deps from python-requirements.txt"
  python -m pip install -U pip "setuptools<66.0.0"
  cp python-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
  python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re

path = Path("/tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt")
lines = []
for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    stripped = line.strip()
    if stripped in {
        "types-dataclasses",
        "types-pkg_resources",
    }:
        continue
    line = re.sub(r'(#egg=[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\s+[<>=!~].*', r'\1', line)
    lines.append(line)
path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
PY
  python -m pip install -r /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt --no-warn-script-location
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[ERROR] python-requirements.txt not found at d08cfa77da7116c03c3a9dd085023cbe5e48f3ae"
  exit 1
fi

# Stage 4: install RISC-V toolchain + Verible, then persist their PATH
if [[ -f util/get-toolchain.py ]]; then
  toolchain_version=""
  if [[ -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
    toolchain_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
  fi

  echo "[INFO] Installing RISC-V toolchain via util/get-toolchain.py"
  if [[ -n "$toolchain_version" ]]; then
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update -r "$toolchain_version"
  else
    echo "[WARN] RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION not found; falling back to util/get-toolchain.py defaults"
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update
  fi
else
  echo "[WARN] util/get-toolchain.py not found at d08cfa77da7116c03c3a9dd085023cbe5e48f3ae; skipping RISC-V toolchain install"
fi

verible_version=""
if [[ -f hw/tool_requirements.py ]]; then
  verible_version="$(python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

ns = {}
exec(Path("hw/tool_requirements.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), ns)
reqs = ns.get("__TOOL_REQUIREMENTS__", {})
entry = reqs.get("verible", "")
if isinstance(entry, dict):
    print(entry.get("min_version", ""))
elif isinstance(entry, str):
    print(entry)
PY
)"
fi
if [[ -z "$verible_version" && -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
  verible_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG VERIBLE_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
fi

if [[ -n "$verible_version" ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Verible ${verible_version}"
  rm -rf /tools/verible
  mkdir -p /tools/verible

  verible_urls=(
    "https://github.com/chipsalliance/verible/releases/download/${verible_version}/verible-${verible_version}-linux-static-x86_64.tar.gz"
    "https://github.com/chipsalliance/verible/releases/download/${verible_version}/verible-${verible_version}-Ubuntu-18.04-bionic-x86_64.tar.gz"
  )

  verible_ready=0
  for verible_url in "${verible_urls[@]}"; do
    if curl -f -Ls -o /tmp/verible.tar.gz "${verible_url}"; then
      tar -C /tools/verible -xf /tmp/verible.tar.gz --strip-components=1
      rm -f /tmp/verible.tar.gz
      verible_ready=1
      break
    fi
  done

  if [[ "${verible_ready}" -ne 1 ]]; then
    echo "[WARN] Failed to download Verible ${verible_version}; continuing without Verible"
    rm -rf /tools/verible
    rm -f /tmp/verible.tar.gz
  fi
else
  echo "[WARN] Unable to determine Verible version from hw/tool_requirements.py or util/container/Dockerfile"
fi

cat > /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh <<'EOF'
for d in /tools/riscv/bin /tools/verible/bin; do
  [ -d "$d" ] && export PATH="$d:$PATH"
done
EOF

if ! grep -q "/etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" /etc/opentitan_bash_env; then
  echo "source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" >> /etc/opentitan_bash_env
fi
source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh

python -m pip show edalize fusesoc hjson >/dev/null
if command -v riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[INFO] RISC-V toolchain ready: $(riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc --version | head -n1)"
else
  echo "[WARN] riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc not found after Stage 4"
fi
if command -v verible-verilog-lint >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[INFO] Verible ready: $(verible-verilog-lint --version | head -n1)"
else
  echo "[WARN] verible-verilog-lint not found after Stage 4"
fi
problem_statement:
## Description
The SRAM Controller (`sram_ctrl`) can leave its memory TileLink Uncached Lightweight (TL-UL) interface stuck when a global life cycle (LC) escalation overlaps with a partial SRAM write. In `sram_ctrl`, a partial write such as a byte write is handled as an internal read-modify-write (RMW) sequence, so a TL-UL request may already be accepted while its internal writeback is still pending.

## Expected Behavior
Once `sram_ctrl` has accepted a memory TL-UL request, LC escalation must not leave that request permanently outstanding. If escalation occurs while a partial write's internal RMW sequence is still in progress, the controller must still return a TL-UL completion response for that already accepted request. Requests that arrive only after escalation has taken effect may be blocked or may return an error response, but previously accepted requests must not hang.

## Actual Behavior
If global LC escalation arrives while `sram_ctrl` is in the middle of the internal RMW sequence for a previously accepted partial write, the request can stall and never produce a TL-UL response. The memory TL-UL interface remains stuck with an outstanding transaction.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the `sram_ctrl` memory datapath that handles partial-write RMW operations together with LC escalation handling on the memory TL-UL interface.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when a global LC escalation request overlaps with a previously accepted partial SRAM write, such as a byte write, whose internal RMW writeback has not yet completed.

title: [kmac] Latch non-zero status of wait timer
body: A fix suggestion for #16716.

[kmac] Latch non-zero status of wait timer

Fixes #16716.

Signed-off-by: Fatih Balli <fatihballi@google.com>

resolved_issues.title: [kmac] Timer expire fires when changing `wait_timer` value on the fly
resolved_issues.body:
Hey @eunchan,

I have a case here that triggers `ErrWaitTimerExpired` error unexpected.

Sequence:
1). Set mode to `EntropyModeEdn`.
2). Disable EDN timer by setting the `wait_timer` to 0.
3). During EDN request, update the timer value to `wait_timer` = 'h28de.
4). KMAC immediately returns a `ErrWaitTimerExpired`.

I think the issue is here:
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/kmac/rtl/kmac_entropy.sv#L625
`timer_expired` is always 1 because the `wait_timer` was set to 0.
Then when changing the `wait_timer` field, the `wait_timer_limit_i` changed from 0 to a non-zero value, which triggers this error.

Waves:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11466553/206300022-6996870d-2c44-4132-864c-fe3979435a02.png)

Reproduce:
 ../../../../util/dvsim/dvsim.py kmac_masked_sim_cfg.hjson -i kmac_masked_entropy_refresh --reseed 1 --seeds 4027977692 -w fsdb

With PR: https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/16714

fix_patch:
diff --git a/hw/ip/kmac/data/kmac.hjson b/hw/ip/kmac/data/kmac.hjson
index 89acde9f8c822..f85d54b09c054 100644
--- a/hw/ip/kmac/data/kmac.hjson
+++ b/hw/ip/kmac/data/kmac.hjson
@@ -688,6 +688,8 @@
           after it sends request to EDN module. If the timer expires, the
           entropy module moves to an error state and notifies to the system.
 
+          If there is a pending EDN request during wait timer update, then this update is delayed until the EDN request is complete.
+
           If 0, the entropy module waits the EDN response always. If EDN does
           not respond in this configuration, the software shall reset the IP.
           '''
diff --git a/hw/ip/kmac/doc/theory_of_operation.md b/hw/ip/kmac/doc/theory_of_operation.md
index 8f418334bd3d7..137acaa26b5b0 100644
--- a/hw/ip/kmac/doc/theory_of_operation.md
+++ b/hw/ip/kmac/doc/theory_of_operation.md
@@ -358,8 +358,9 @@ The request is dropped by the KMAC_APP module.
 The lower 3 bits of [`ERR_CODE`](data/kmac.hjson#err_code) contains the received command from the SW.
 #### WaitTimerExpired (0x04)
 
-The SW may set the EDN wait timer to exit from EDN request state if the response from EDN takes long.
-If the timer expires, the module cancels the transaction and report the `WaitTimerExpired` error.
+The timer values set by SW is internally used only when pending EDN request is completed.
+Therefore, dynamically changing wait timer cannot be used as a way to poke the timer out of a stalling EDN request.
+If a non-zero timer expires, the module cancels the transaction and reports the `WaitTimerExpired` error.
 
 When this error happens, the state machine in KMAC_ENTROPY module moves to Wait state.
 In that state, it keeps using the pre-generated entropy and asserting the entropy valid signal.
diff --git a/hw/ip/kmac/rtl/kmac_entropy.sv b/hw/ip/kmac/rtl/kmac_entropy.sv
index c5c307a180c5f..9db331713ebeb 100644
--- a/hw/ip/kmac/rtl/kmac_entropy.sv
+++ b/hw/ip/kmac/rtl/kmac_entropy.sv
@@ -230,6 +230,26 @@ module kmac_entropy
   // Datapath //
   //////////////
 
+  // For latching (`wait_timer_limit_i` != 0) during last `timer_update`
+  // See #16716
+  logic non_zero_wait_timer_limit;
+  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
+    if (!rst_ni) begin
+      non_zero_wait_timer_limit <= '0;
+    end else if (timer_update) begin
+      non_zero_wait_timer_limit <= |wait_timer_limit_i;
+    end
+  end
+
+  logic [TimerPrescalerW-1:0] wait_timer_prescaler_d;
+  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
+    if (!rst_ni) begin
+      wait_timer_prescaler_d <= '0;
+    end else if (timer_update) begin
+      wait_timer_prescaler_d <= wait_timer_prescaler_i;
+    end
+  end
+
   // Timers ===================================================================
   always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
     if (!rst_ni) begin
@@ -262,7 +282,7 @@ module kmac_entropy
     end else if (timer_update) begin
       prescaler_cnt <= wait_timer_prescaler_i;
     end else if (timer_enable && prescaler_cnt == '0) begin
-      prescaler_cnt <= wait_timer_prescaler_i;
+      prescaler_cnt <= wait_timer_prescaler_d;
     end else if (timer_enable) begin
       prescaler_cnt <= prescaler_cnt - 1'b 1;
     end
@@ -622,7 +642,7 @@ module kmac_entropy
         // Wait timer
         timer_enable = 1'b 1;
 
-        if (timer_expired && |wait_timer_limit_i) begin
+        if (timer_expired && non_zero_wait_timer_limit) begin
           // If timer count is non-zero and expired;
           st_d = StRandErrWaitExpired;

problem_statement:
## Description
The KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) IP has a bug in its entropy acquisition path to the EDN (Entropy Distribution Network). In `EntropyModeEdn` (the mode where KMAC requests entropy from EDN), software uses `entropy_period.wait_timer` to control how long KMAC waits for an EDN response before reporting `ErrWaitTimerExpired`; a value of 0 disables that timeout. If software issues an EDN entropy request with `wait_timer` set to 0 and then rewrites `entropy_period.wait_timer` to a non-zero value while that same EDN request is still pending, KMAC can treat the already outstanding request as if its wait timer had expired.

## Expected Behavior
Changing `entropy_period.wait_timer` from 0 to a non-zero value while an EDN request is already outstanding must not cause `ErrWaitTimerExpired` for that in-flight request. A request that started while the wait timer was disabled must continue waiting for the EDN response and complete without a wait-timer-expired error if the EDN response arrives. `ErrWaitTimerExpired` should only be reported for an EDN wait interval during which a non-zero timeout was already in effect and that timeout actually expires.

## Actual Behavior
If an EDN request is pending and software rewrites `entropy_period.wait_timer` from 0 to a non-zero value before the EDN response arrives, KMAC can immediately report `ErrWaitTimerExpired` even though the outstanding request started with the timeout disabled and the newly written non-zero timeout has not elapsed.

## Affected Function
This affects the KMAC entropy acquisition logic that waits for EDN responses in `EntropyModeEdn`, specifically the handling of `entropy_period.wait_timer` for an outstanding EDN request.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when KMAC is operating in `EntropyModeEdn`, `entropy_period.wait_timer` is 0 when an EDN entropy request becomes outstanding, and software changes `entropy_period.wait_timer` to a non-zero value before that same request receives its EDN response.

title: [kmac] Zero capacity of KMAC against SW (sideload only)
body:
One possible low-cost way to fix #17508. At the end of KMAC operation, it zeroes the capacity part of Keccak state that is passed to TL-UL primitives.

Few questions that I'm asking myself about this PR and the main issue:

- Is `kmac_app` is the right submodule to do this?
- Should we also try to raise an error if SW tries to read from capacity? At the moment, I do not see a good error flow to realize this, so I felt this would be a high effort. I also do not see any security benefit.
- Should we harden this zeroing mechanism? With FI, one can flip the select signal that goes into MUX. Plus, this signal propagates all the way from registers into this MUX circuit, so there is a large exposure.

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[kmac] Prevent SW from reading capacity for sideloaded KMAC

Fixes #17508.

If we let SW read the capacity at the end of KMAC operation,
then SW can recompute the preceeding Keccak states. This allows
SW to recompute the sideloaded key. This PR prevents reading
capacity for sideloaded KMAC operations.

Signed-off-by: Fatih Balli <fatihballi@google.com>

resolved_issues.title: [kmac] Prevent SW from reading capacity
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

I think `kmac` should prevent SW from reading `capacity` (the last 2*sec_str bits) of Keccak state.

In the scenario `kmac` is using a sideloaded key from `keymgr`, we want to hide the key from SW. There should not be a way for SW to read or compute the sideloaded key, because it is a key directly managed by `keymgr`.

The one-way security of the KMAC algorithm relies on the assumption that the attacker only sees the output of the algorithm, and not the full state of Keccak reached at the end of the operation. The output of KMAC is basically read from the `rate` part of Keccak state, and `capacity` remains secret.

If we let the attacker also read the `capacity` part of Keccak state, then it is possible to simply compute the previous Keccak states by executing inverse Keccak permutation. For instance, given full Keccak state for `KMAC(secret_key || known_val)`, one can compute `secret_key`.

It might be a good idea to prevent SW to read `capacity` part of Keccak. What do you folks think?

cc: @vogelpi @cindychip @johannheyszl

problem_statement:
## Description
The KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) accelerator exposes a software-readable `STATE` window containing the terminal 1600-bit Keccak state for software-driven operations. When the operation uses a sideloaded secret key from the Key Manager, this visibility is too broad: software can read the Keccak capacity portion of the state, even though only the output-bearing rate portion should be visible.

## Expected Behavior
For a KMAC operation that uses a sideloaded Key Manager key, once the terminal Keccak state becomes readable through the `STATE` window, software should still be able to read the rate portion used to obtain the digest, but it must not be able to read the capacity portion. The capacity is the last `2 * security_strength` bits of the 1600-bit Keccak state. For operations that do not use a sideloaded key, the software-visible state should remain unchanged.

## Actual Behavior
When a sideloaded-key KMAC operation reaches the software-visible state/output phase, reading the `STATE` window returns the full terminal Keccak state, including the capacity bits. Exposing the full state breaks the assumption that an attacker sees only the KMAC output; with a known message, the extra state visibility can allow software to work backward through the Keccak permutation and recover information about the sideloaded secret key.

## Affected Functionality
This affects the KMAC accelerator's software-visible state path for software-driven operations that use a Key Manager sideloaded key.

## Trigger Condition
This issue is triggered when software starts a KMAC operation with a sideloaded secret key from the Key Manager, the operation reaches the phase where the terminal Keccak state is exposed through the `STATE` window, and software reads that state. In that situation, the capacity portion becomes visible even though it should remain hidden.

title: Add write enable to guard SW-initiated LC controller states transition
body: LC controller allows state transitions by means of configuring the transition interface CSRs via JTAG (physical access) or SW (which can be remotely); this leaves the transition interface vulnerable to remote DoS attacks, e.g., transitioning to SCRAP - see  #17118. This adds a 1-bit register enable SW_TRANSITION_EN that allows SW transitions by default, and can be cleared by privileged software or JTAG to disable SW LC state transitions.

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
Add write enable to guard SW-initiated LC ctrl states transition

This adds a 1-bit register enable CLAIM_TRANSITION_IF_REGWEN that acts as the write enable for the hardware mutex register CLAIM_TRANSITION_IF. When cleared to 0, the mutex register cannot be written to anymore, thus disabling SW-initiated lifecycle state transitions.

Signed-off-by: Ghada Dessouky <gdessouky@google.com>
Co-authored-by: Chris Frantz <cfrantz@google.com>

resolved_issues.title: [lc_ctrl] Remote DoS attacks
resolved_issues.body:
The life cycle state of an OT device can transition to `SCRAP` from any state, by means of configuring the life cycle controller CSRs via SW or JTAG. While this is not an attack that enables privileged access to assets, it brings the device to a permanently terminal state = DoS.  In an offline discussion with @msfschaffner, we realize that if an attacker manages to gain privileged access (by means of SW vulnerabilities) to the system bus and can write transactions to it, then various remote Denial-of-Service attacks would be possible; transition to `SCRAP` would then only be one such example.

Does it make sense to discuss this further and evaluate whether we need to consider such class of attacks and if additional hardening countermeasures to the system bus or otherwise are necessary? Also are these attacks a concern/requirement for certification?

@johannheyszl @moidx @msfschaffner @tjaychen 

> estimate 16

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan Life Cycle Controller (`lc_ctrl`) exposes a life cycle transition interface through memory-mapped control and status registers (CSRs) on the system bus and through the Joint Test Action Group (JTAG) interface. Because that interface can request irreversible life cycle transitions such as the terminal `SCRAP` state, leaving the software-visible CSR path always re-openable creates a remote denial-of-service (DoS) risk if an attacker gains privileged software access to the system bus.

## Expected Behavior
There must be a way to disable software-initiated access to the `lc_ctrl` transition interface. After privileged software has locked out further software claims, later system-bus writes must no longer be able to claim the `CLAIM_TRANSITION_IF` hardware mutex. In particular, after software has claimed and then released the transition interface, a later write to `CLAIM_TRANSITION_IF` must be ignored, the register must read back as 0, and `TRANSITION_REGWEN` must remain 0 so the transition interface does not become writable from the software-visible CSR path again.

## Actual Behavior
In the current implementation, the software-visible claim path is always available. Privileged software with system-bus write access can write `CLAIM_TRANSITION_IF`, make the claim stick, and cause `TRANSITION_REGWEN` to become 1. Even after the mutex has been released, nothing prevents software from claiming it again, so the transition interface can be reopened from the system bus and the remote DoS path remains available.

## Affected Function
This affects the `lc_ctrl` software-accessible life cycle transition interface, specifically the system-bus claim mutex (`CLAIM_TRANSITION_IF`) and the hardware write-enable (`TRANSITION_REGWEN`) that gates the transition interface CSRs.

## Trigger Condition
The issue is triggered when privileged software can write to the `lc_ctrl` CSRs over the system bus and attempts to claim or re-claim the transition interface. The important boundary condition is a second software claim after the interface has already been claimed once and then released: once software-initiated transitions have been locked out, that later claim must not succeed and must not make `TRANSITION_REGWEN` go high again.

## Implementation Constraint
The software-visible claim path for life-cycle transitions should add a dedicated write-enable control whose identifier includes the exact token `claim_transition_if_regwen`. This control must be separate from `TRANSITION_REGWEN` and must prevent later software writes from re-claiming `CLAIM_TRANSITION_IF` once software lockout is active.

title: [csrng] Define, fix, and verify `cs_aes_halt`
body:
This PR:
- Adds a minimal specification of CSRNG's behavior on the `cs_aes_halt` interface.
- Fixes the acknowledge output of `cs_aes_halt` driven by CSRNG to be level instead of pulse.
- Configures CSRNG's DV so that it does not deassert the request of `cs_aes_halt` after a single acknowledge cycle.
- Adds assertions to CSRNG RTL to ensure its AES is only active while `cs_aes_halt` is not.

Tested locally with a full regression run of CSRNG. The added assertion never failed and all test results are in line with current nightly results.

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[csrng/doc] Specify behavior around `cs_aes_halt`

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

[csrng/rtl] Fix `cs_aes_halt_ack` for four-phase HS

The `cs_aes_halt` interface follows a four-phase handshake protocol.
This implies that `ack` does not drop before `req`.  The current CSRNG
code, which originated from #10830, violates this condition.  This
commit fixes that.

This will be made visible in DV with the subsequent commit.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

[csrng/dv] Use four-phase HS for `cs_aes_halt`

Prior to this commit, the request signal of `cs_aes_halt`, which gets
driven by a DV agent, would drop as soon as CSRNG had set acknowledge
high for a single cycle.  This does not correspond to how `entropy_src`,
which usually drives the request signal, would necessarily behave.
Instead, `entropy_src` could keep the request asserted for many cycles
after CSRNG has acknowledged it.

By changing the agent to a four-phase handshake, the agent can now also
keep the request high after the acknowledge.  This would expose the bug
fixed by the previous commit.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

[csrng] Add assertions for `cs_aes_halt` and AES activity

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: [csrng/rtl] Change cs_aes_halt_o to a pulse
resolved_issues.body:
To be able to reuse the DV req/ack module for this simple interface,
the cs_aes_halt_o will be a single clock in pulse size.

Signed-off-by: Mark Branstad <mark.branstad@wdc.com>

--- a/hw/ip/csrng/data/csrng.hjson
+++ b/hw/ip/csrng/data/csrng.hjson
@@ -91,6 +91,10 @@
       name:    "cs_aes_halt"
       act:     "rsp"
       package: "entropy_src_pkg"
+      desc:    '''
+               Coordinate activity between CSRNG's AES and Entropy Source's SHA3.
+               When CSRNG gets a request and its AES is not active, it acknowledges and until the request has dropped neither runs its AES nor drops the acknowledge.
+               '''

problem_statement:
The bug is in the CSRNG (Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generator) core's `cs_aes_halt` request/acknowledge interface with the Entropy Source IP. This interface is used when the Entropy Source asks CSRNG to enter a halted state before the Entropy Source performs SHA3 work.

The affected behavior is CSRNG's generation of `cs_aes_halt_ack`. Once the Entropy Source asserts `cs_aes_halt_req` and CSRNG has completed any in-flight AES activity, CSRNG is expected to assert `cs_aes_halt_ack` and keep that acknowledge asserted until the requester deasserts `cs_aes_halt_req`. `cs_aes_halt_ack` must therefore behave as a level-sensitive acknowledge for a four-phase handshake, not as a one-cycle pulse.

CSRNG currently acknowledges the request with a single-cycle pulse. If `cs_aes_halt_req` remains high after that first acknowledge cycle, `cs_aes_halt_ack` drops on the next cycle even though the request is still asserted. This prematurely ends the acknowledged-halt state from the requester's point of view.

The failure is triggered when the Entropy Source keeps `cs_aes_halt_req` asserted for multiple cycles after CSRNG first acknowledges it, instead of dropping the request immediately. This includes the boundary case where the halt request arrives while CSRNG is still finishing current work and then remains asserted after CSRNG becomes idle enough to acknowledge it.

title: [csrng, rtl] Remove some unneeded I/O muxes
body: As discussed previously in the Sec WG, this resolves #16564.

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[csrng, rtl] Remove output mux on genbits bus

This output mux is not functionally required but poses an FI target.
Therefore, it has been decided to remove it. Related to that, the output
assertions are modified to use the valid bit as enable term.

This related to lowRISC/OpenTitan#16564.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

[csrng, rtl] Simplify main input mux

Previously, this main entropy mux had multiple all-zero inputs that were
not actually required from a functionality perspective. The only case
where the design needs the input to be really zero is when flag0 is set.

This commit thus implements the following changes to the mux:
1. Reduce the number of all-zero inputs (lower FI attack surface). The
   only all-zero input is when the FI-hardened flag0 field is set.
2. Only flop new input from entropy source if an entropy request is
   actually outstanding. Previously, a glitch on the acknowledge line
   would have caused CSRNG to flop whatever was on the bus (it wouldn't
   necessarily have been consumed downstream though).

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#16564.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: [csrng] Should we remove some I/O muxes?
resolved_issues.body:
During the V2/V2S work I noticed that inside CSRNG there are two muxes that are potentially problematic for FI and I was wondering if we should do something about them.

The first one is on the genbits output to the software interface and the command stages:
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/12c8613ab849d256aea590f0a509166193d3b2b0/hw/ip/csrng/rtl/csrng_core.sv#L971

The problem I see with that is that most of the time, CSRNG will output a constant value here. Using a glitch in the downstream logic (e.g. EDN) this constant value can get sampled. Repetition checks don't necessarily help here, only if they're done on a 32-bit granularity in the consumer (which we not always do). I think we just remove this mux as we did with various output muxes of FIFOs in the same path.

The second mux is on the `entropy_src_seed_d` buffer (this basically buffers the entropy input to CSRNG):
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/12c8613ab849d256aea590f0a509166193d3b2b0/hw/ip/csrng/rtl/csrng_core.sv#L1245-L1251

This mux seems to be required for correct functionality. However, the problem I see is that several inputs are zero/constant and there seems to be no hardening on the mux. This could potentially be exploited to blank the entropy input to CSRNG which would be very bad. I am not sure how to best protect against this but I think we should do something about it. It's probably best to discuss this in the security team after the break.

> estimate 8
> remaining 2023-04-20 6

problem_statement:
## Description
In the Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generator (CSRNG) IP, the command-stage `genbits` response interface does not preserve the status of the last generated word across a dequeue boundary. The affected interface is the CSRNG command stage output seen by software or application consumers: `genbits_valid` indicates whether a staged 128-bit word is available, `genbits_bus` carries that word, and `genbits_fips` carries the associated status bit.

## Expected Behavior
After a `genbits` word has been staged and then consumed, `genbits_valid` should deassert on the next cycle, but the interface should continue to present the last staged word and its associated `genbits_fips` status bit until a later word overwrites them. Whether the values are currently consumable must be determined only by `genbits_valid`; deasserting `genbits_valid` must not itself clear the held status bit.

## Actual Behavior
When the staged word is consumed and `genbits_valid` goes low, the command-stage logic drives `genbits_fips` low immediately instead of retaining the last staged status bit on the idle cycle after the dequeue.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when CSRNG has queued a `genbits` word with `genbits_fips` asserted, the consumer accepts that word, and the interface transitions from `genbits_valid = 1` to `genbits_valid = 0` on the following cycle.

title: [lc_ctrl] Fix bugs in volatile unlock mechanism
body:
A few alignments are needed:
- The LC counter may already have been incremented by unsuccessful unlock operations. Hence forcing to `LcCnt1` as part of the volatile unlock could result in programming errors when further transitions are attempted. The solution is to force to `LcCnt1` only in the case when the counter is `LcCnt0`. 
- The continuous state vector sampling needs to be disabled after a volatile unlock - otherwise the LC_CTRL would revert to RAW immediately after 1 cycle. This mechanism was there before, but it had a bug that is fixed here.
- Suggested doc updates from https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/18248 are incorporated.
- An SVA inside pinmux that makes sure the straps are only sampled once is fixed.

2) the count was always forced to 1 as part of the volatile unlock
   operation. this may cause problems if previous regular (but
   unsuccessful) unlock operations already incremented the counter

resolved_issues.title: [lc_ctrl] Add raw unlock bypass for test chips
resolved_issues.body:
This adds a volatile RAW -> TEST_UNLOCKED0 mechanism for test chips.

This solution does NOT use KMAC token hashing, hence the RTL diff is smaller. An alternative implementation with KMAC hashing is drafted in #18238 for reference. This has been discussed with @cdgori and we decided not to  pursue that since the RTL diff is too big and would add significant risk. The direct comparison without hashing is acceptable since the mechanism will not be compiled into PROD silicon.

Note that the modifications in pinmux are needed so that the hardware straps can be re-sampled in order to ungate the DFT and RISC-V TAPs.

Addresses https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/18246

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan Life Cycle Controller (LC_CTRL) supports a volatile `RAW -> TEST_UNLOCKED0` transition on test-chip configurations. In this mode, LC_CTRL temporarily exposes `TEST_UNLOCKED0` without programming the One-Time Programmable (OTP) life cycle state, so software can use the unlocked state immediately after the transition succeeds.

## Expected Behavior
If the device starts in `RAW` with life cycle transition count `LcCnt0`, and software successfully requests a volatile transition to `TEST_UNLOCKED0` using the correct raw unlock token, LC_CTRL must continue reporting `TEST_UNLOCKED0` in subsequent cycles after the transition completes. In the same scenario, the reported transition count must advance to `LcCnt1` and remain `LcCnt1` while the volatile unlocked state is active; it must not fall back to the OTP-backed `RAW` / `LcCnt0` view on the next idle cycle.

## Actual Behavior
After a nominally successful volatile `RAW -> TEST_UNLOCKED0` transition, LC_CTRL resumes sampling the OTP-backed life cycle state and transition count. Because OTP still contains `RAW` and `LcCnt0`, the externally visible state can revert almost immediately after the transition, so later reads report `RAW` and `LcCnt0` instead of preserving the volatile `TEST_UNLOCKED0` state.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the LC_CTRL volatile raw unlock path for the `RAW -> TEST_UNLOCKED0` transition, specifically the logic that decides whether the post-transition life cycle state and transition count should continue to come from the volatile unlock result or from ongoing OTP sampling.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when volatile raw unlock is supported, the device is currently in `RAW` with count `LcCnt0`, software claims the LC_CTRL transition interface, enables volatile raw unlock, targets `TEST_UNLOCKED0`, provides the correct raw unlock token, and starts the transition. The failure is visible in the first later idle cycles after the transition completes.

title: [usbdev] Remove data toggle clear in suspend
body:
The link_active_i term was misplaced, and data toggles should not be cleared in suspended state. In fact, they should be retained, and usbdev will need to give software greater visibility and control, so it can save / restore state in coordination with deep sleep.

For the purposes of an ECO, leave link_active_i unused. It was intended to help prevent the packet engines from responding to packets and dirtying FIFOs before software is ready, but that is left for a later commit.

Found by @alees24 in #18940

resolved_issues.title: [usbdev] USB device clears Data Toggle flag when link inactive (Suspend-Resume)
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

When the device detects a link inactive state the OUT side clears its Data Toggle flag. The IN side leaves its flag untouched.
The result is that following Resume from the Suspended state the first _new_ data packet transmitted to a non-Control endpoint may be ACKed by the device and the data is dropped, on the assumption that this is a _re-transmission_ of the previous packet.

This is true for all endpoints, but we may assume that for Control Transfers the first thing to be transmitted will be a SETUP packet so the issue should not be seen. For Bulk Transfers such as serial port traffic, re-opening the serial port connection following a suspend-resume cycle may result in the first OUT packet (host->device) being dropped because the Linux Host Controller/driver stack still has knowledge of the previous state and the first data packet will sometimes be transmitted with a DATA1 token.

From my reading of the USB 2.0 specification the toggle state is cleared to DATA0 when the endpoint is configured but should be unaffected by device Suspend/Resume. @a-will Is this correct? What is the history of resetting in response to 'not link_active_i' please?

**RTL**:

usb_fs_nb_out_pe.sv: 354
```
    end else if (link_reset_i || !link_active_i) begin
      data_toggle_q <= '0; // All endpoints
```
Suggested change for **partial mitigation**:
```
    end else if (link_reset_i) begin
      data_toggle_q <= '0; // All endpoints
```
matching the comparable logic in usb_fs_nb_in_pe.sv.

_This works for any Suspend-Resume signaling that the host performs automatically, but currently we cannot reinstate the Data Toggle states upon returning from a Sleep state. There is no register interface either for reading the current toggles or for setting them. The software is only able to clear the toggles._

Both IN and OUT traffic will suffer from this issue when returning from a Sleep state.

**Other workarounds:**

Avoid suspending, or when there is a suspicion that the host may have requested the device suspend, force a reset of the device. This can be achieved if talking to the device using libusb, but not - as far as I know - when using regular serial port traffic via open/read/write/close.

**Background**:

Streaming data test (usbdev_stream_test) normally sends PRND packets from device (IN) to host where they are checked, combined with another PRND stream and returned to the device (OUT) where they are checked against expectations. The Linux driver stack will not auto-suspend a device that has active connections, but I have modified the host-side code of this test to close its file descriptors/libusb usage, instruct the driver stack to suspend the device, and then to resume it, before re-establishing the connections to the device.

The first packet received after re-establishing the Bulk transfer connections to the device has a 50% chance of a DATA1 PID being used, in which case the logic analyzer shows the packet being transmitted to the device and ACKed, but no buffer is consumed within the device and the packet is just dropped internally. The checking code then objects to the next lump of data that is received because part of the expected PRND stream has not arrived.

This happens whether I'm using libusb or whether I'm using the 'open/read/write/close' kernel functions to access the device via /dev/ttyUSBn as regular serial ports.

My host-side code, when modified to perform Suspend-Resume signaling frequently can induce a test failure within 15-30 seconds. Introducing a bodge which sends a dummy packet when it knows the first post-Resume packet shall be sent with DATA1 allows the test to continue running for at least 45 minutes without failure. It can do this only because it can control exactly how many packets have been sent, but in so doing it is also severely limiting the bandwidth. This is not a practical fix.


@msfschaffner  @johngt @GregAC

problem_statement:
## Description
In the OpenTitan USB device (USBDEV) IP, the receive-side data-toggle state for non-control OUT endpoints is cleared when the USB link becomes inactive during suspend. This state is used by the USB device OUT packet engine to distinguish a new packet from a retransmission. As a result, after suspend and resume, the first new OUT packet can be acknowledged but not committed to the endpoint buffer.

## Expected Behavior
Suspend and resume, without a USB bus reset, must preserve the current data-toggle value for each non-control OUT endpoint. If an endpoint successfully accepts a DATA0 packet before suspend, it must still expect DATA1 after resume. A valid DATA1 packet received after resume must be treated as new data, written into the endpoint buffer, and advance the endpoint's data-toggle state.

## Trigger Condition
The failure occurs on a non-control OUT endpoint after it has already accepted a DATA0 packet, the USB link then enters the inactive/suspended state, and the link later resumes without a bus reset. In that scenario, a host that correctly continues with DATA1 can have the first post-resume OUT packet acknowledged by the device but effectively dropped.

title: [usbdev] Truncate RX after receiving a PRE PID
body:
Trigger EOP response when the receiver sees a PRE PID. Because the preamble is not a full packet and does not terminate with an EOP until after the low-speed transmission is complete, stop processing the packet immediately after receiving the PID. The low-speed portion of the packet will trigger error conditions otherwise.

Resolves #19148

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[usbdev] Truncate RX after receiving a PRE PID

Trigger EOP response when the receiver sees a PRE PID. Because the
preamble is not a full packet and does not terminate with an EOP until
after the low-speed transmission is complete, stop processing the packet
immediately after receiving the PID. The low-speed portion of the packet
will trigger error conditions otherwise.

Signed-off-by: Alexander Williams <awill@opentitan.org>

resolved_issues.title: [usbdev] Forwarded Low Speed traffic raises bit stuffing errors
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

This is more an imperfection than a fault; when our Full Speed device is connected to a hub that is operating in Full/Low Speed mode - because it has no High Speed devices connected - the Low Speed traffic to a device connected alongside usbdev is forwarded to our device with a 'PRE' special packet that prefixes the Low Speed transmission. This results in usbdev attempting to interpret the packet data and raising a 'Bit Stuffing error' to the software.

Suggestion: for this release, software should disable the 'rx_bitstuff_err' interrupt to avoid wasting CPU time responding to spurious interrupts. For the future, the RTL should probably be modified to handle this case more cleanly.

Low Speed devices are typically budget keyboards and mice using Interrupt transfer types; this issue was identified when connecting usbdev to a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B alongside an inexpensive keyboard and mouse setup. Connecting them through an additional USB3-capable Hub prevented the Bit Stuffing errors from occurring.


Details:

Our usbdev logic has no awareness of the PRE special packet. This special PID is not followed by any data bytes, CRC5 or even an End Of Packet; instead the Hub Setup time of **>= 4 Full Speed** bit intervals of **Idle** state ensues, followed by the Low Speed SYNC. This means that either the Idle period or the first Low Speed bit of the SYNC signal causes usbdev to raise a Bit Stuffing error.

Since the bit stuffing error leads to usbdev deciding that the packet has ended, and valid Low Speed data cannot look like a valid SYNC field, the device safely discards the rest of the Low Speed transaction. It's perhaps worth mentioning that usbdev does not see any of the responses from the Low Speed devices; just the downstream-directed Host transmissions within each transaction.

DPI model has been modified to generate this test case, for reproducing the bit stuffing errors in simulation. The top-level test _usbdev_exc_test_ (WIP) now also exercises the propagation of Low Speed SETUP, OUT and IN transactions, switching the bus traffic between Full and Low Speed modes as per real physical hosts.

This diagram captures the real traffic sent from the RPi 4 host controller:
![PRE_Low_cropped](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/assets/117650394/c464e657-7b80-41c0-a9e3-a0d8a7966c98)

For further details see section **8.6.5 Low Speed Transactions** in the USB 2.0 Specification.
