problem_statement:
## Description
The USB device (`usbdev`) IP's full-speed receive path does not correctly handle the USB 2.0 `PRE` preamble packet identifier (PID) that a hub uses before forwarding low-speed traffic. When a full-speed OpenTitan device is attached through a hub that also serves low-speed peripherals, the hub can place a valid `PRE` PID on the full-speed segment and then continue with low-speed signaling intended for another device. The affected function is the `usbdev` full-speed RX path and its packet-end/error handling after a PID has been decoded.

## Expected Behavior
After the full-speed receive path has accepted a valid `PRE` PID, it should treat that PID as the end of the full-speed reception: it should terminate the current packet immediately, ignore the following low-speed signaling that belongs to another downstream device, and avoid reporting a bit-stuffing error for that forwarded traffic.

## Actual Behavior
`usbdev` keeps decoding bus activity after the `PRE` PID as if it were still part of a normal full-speed packet. The subsequent forwarded low-speed signaling is then misinterpreted, and the receiver reports a spurious bit-stuffing error to software.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when `usbdev` is operating as a full-speed USB device behind a hub that forwards low-speed traffic, and the receiver sees a valid packet start plus a valid `PRE` PID before additional line activity from the forwarded low-speed transaction arrives. In that boundary case, the receiver should end the full-speed packet at `PRE`, but instead it continues decoding the later signaling and raises a false bit-stuffing error.

resolved_issues.title: [edn] Don't propagate SW commands after a fatal error
resolved_issues.body:
bad029c9c7 fixes the propagation of SW commands, so that writes to the `SW_CMD_REQ` register don’t propagate in multiple Auto mode states. The default assignment in EDN’s main FSM still allows the propagation of SW commands, though, and these default assignments apply even to the fatal error state. **Thus, SW can send commands to CSRNG even if EDN is in the fatal error state.** A CSRNG command that returns `genbits` will get those bits stored in EDN’s internal FIFOs. EDN’s endpoints cannot access the entropy in the fatal error state, however, because the acknowledge FSM stops acknowledging requests. We don’t test this case currently, but we do have the `EdnFatalAlertNoRsp_A` assertion, which ensures that EDN does not acknowledge any requests in the fatal alert state.

**For D3, we should tweak the main FSM so that it only propagates SW commands when needed (and certainly not in the fatal alert state).**

resolved_issues.title: [edn] Should SW commands be allowed in boot_req_mode
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

In the documentation it says :

> In boot-time request mode, the command sequence is fully hardware-controlled and no command customization is possible. In this mode, the EDN automatically issues a special reduced-latency instantiate command followed by the default generate commands. This means, for instance, that no personalization strings or additional data may be passed to the CSRNG application interface port in this mode. On exiting, the EDN issues an uninstantiate command to destroy the associated CSRNG instance.

However, in the RTL I couldn't find anything that keeps SW commands from being issued in boot_req_mode. I also observed SW commands in the tests while CTRL.BOOT_REQ_MODE was set to true. 

Looking at the RTL code I think it is possible that sw commands can be issued in boot mode. It just relies on the SM not being in any of the following states: AutoSendGenCmd, AutoSendReseedCmd, AutoAckWait, AutoDispatch, AutoCaptGenCnt, AutoCaptReseedCnt, BootSendGenCmd or BootLoadIns. Other than in those states, a sw command can be issued if (reg2hw.sw_cmd_req.qe & sw_cmd_valid) is equal to 1’b1. [This](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/17083/commits/793f168b1e18a00c6f2ce63389668af64b7b0981) commit also aligns with the stated above.

If we decide to change the RTL, [this](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/17083/commits/793f168b1e18a00c6f2ce63389668af64b7b0981) commit could be extended to exclude more states. But in my opinion a cleaner solution could be to add a signal in the main_sm, that is high whenever the sm is in the AutoLoadIns or the SW_Port_Mode state. This way we could disallow sw commands unless the above signal is high.

If we decide to keep things as they are we may consider to adapt the documentation.

Another thing to consider is that the SM is in the BootDone state when the boot sequence is done. It stays there until the EDN is disabled or an error occurs. We could also discuss adding a transition from BootDone to Idle when the CTRL.BOOT_REQ_MODE flag is disabled. This might make the RTL align more with the quote from the documentation below, since atm disabling CTRL.BOOT_REQ_MODE doesn't cause the SM to leave the BootDone state. To my observation, there is also no uninstatiate command being issued when exiting boot mode.

> Once firmware initialization is complete, it is important to exit this mode if the endpoints ever need FIPS-approved random values. This is done by either clearing the EDN_ENABLE field or clearing the BOOT_REQ_MODE field in [CTRL](https://opentitan.org/book/hw/ip/edn/doc/registers.html#ctrl) to halt the boot-time request state machine. Firmware must then wait for successful the shutdown of the state machine by polling the REQ_MODE_SM_STS field of the [SUM_STS](https://opentitan.org/book/hw/ip/edn/doc/registers.html#sum_sts) register.

FYI: @vogelpi @andreaskurth

problem_statement:
## Description
The EDN (Entropy Distribution Network) IP does not cleanly hand control from boot-time request mode back to its normal software command path. After the boot-time sequence finishes, the EDN main state machine reaches `BootDone`; clearing `CTRL.BOOT_REQ_MODE` while keeping the EDN enabled is supposed to exit boot-time request mode and return the block to software-driven operation.

## Expected Behavior
When the boot-time sequence has completed and firmware clears `CTRL.BOOT_REQ_MODE` without disabling the EDN, the EDN main state machine should leave `BootDone`, enter the normal software-port state (`SWPortMode`), and report that the software command interface is ready again so firmware can submit normal post-boot commands through the EDN software port.

## Actual Behavior
After the boot-time sequence completes, clearing `CTRL.BOOT_REQ_MODE` can leave the EDN stuck in `BootDone` instead of transitioning into software-port operation. The software command path therefore does not report ready for normal post-boot commands.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the EDN main state machine path that handles the handoff from boot-time request mode to the normal software-port mode.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when the EDN is enabled in boot-time request mode, the configured boot-time sequence runs to completion, firmware clears `CTRL.BOOT_REQ_MODE` while keeping the EDN enabled, and firmware then attempts to use the EDN software command interface.

title: [edn] Clear auto cmd FIFOs after edn disable
body:
This PR clears the auto cmd FIFOs after the edn is disabled.
For more precise information check out the individual commit messages.

This PR resolves #19653

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[edn] Reset auto cmd FIFOs when EDN is disabled

This commit resets the auto mode cmd FIFOs whenever the EDN is disabled.
This is done by setting the main_sm_done_pulse_o to high whenever the
edn_enable_i signal changes to low. In edn_core.sv, the done_pulse is used
for several purposes other than just resetting the FIFOs. However, this change
has no or little impact for the other three use cases of this signal. In two of
those three cases the done_pulse has no impact, since the EDN is disabled and the
multiplexer ignores the pulse. In the third case the max_num_between_reseeds is
loaded into a counter whenever the done_pulse is high. This should be fine since the
CSRNG is initialized anyways, should the EDN enter auto mode at a later time.
The only difference for the third case would be that when the auto mode is left
through disabling the EDN, the counter is now reset and should it re-enter auto
mode the counter starts counting from 0 again. This didn't use to be the case.

Signed-off-by: Hakim Filali <hfilali@lowrisc.org>

[edn] Get the DV environment in line with resetting FIFOs after EDN is disabled

This commit gets the DV environment in line with the prior change. This includes
waiting for the EDN to be enabled before disabling in edn_disable_auto_req_mode_vseq.
It also includes an update for the tracing of the scoreboard FIFOs.

Signed-off-by: Hakim Filali <hfilali@lowrisc.org>

[edn/doc] Update documentation to explain when auto cmd FIFOs are cleared

This commit updates the documentation to make it more clear when exactly
the auto command FIFOs are cleared.

Signed-off-by: Hakim Filali <hfilali@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: [edn] Discussion on Generate/Reseed cmd FIFOs behavior when disabling EDN
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

Currently the Reseed_cmd and the Generate_cmd FIFOs get cleared whenever the CTRL. CMD_FIFO_RST flag is set to true or when the edn_main_sm generates a done pulse. A done_pulse is generated on 3 different occasions:

1. Then edn_main_sm transitions from the BootPulse to the BootDone state (in boot_req_mode)
2. The edn_main_sm transitions from the AutoDispatch to the Idle state (when auto_req_mode is disabled)
3. The edn_main_sm transitions from the Idle state to the sw_port_mode state (when boot/auto_req_mode are both disabled)

The FIFOs aren't cleared however, when the EDN is disabled. E.g. the transition from the AutoDispatch to the Idle state could also happen when the EDN is disabled. In that case, the FIFOs aren't cleared. Even though it has the same initial and final state as point 2.

We should discuss if this is the intended behavior. And if not, when do we want to clear the FIFOs?

The results of this discussion should be added to the documentation.

FYI: @vogelpi @andreaskurth

problem_statement:
## Description
The bug is in the Entropy Distribution Network (EDN) auto request shutdown path. In auto request mode, EDN stores the programmed `GENERATE_CMD` and `RESEED_CMD` sequences in replay FIFOs so it can resend them to the Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generator (CSRNG). When firmware disables EDN by clearing `CTRL.EDN_ENABLE` while auto request mode is still configured, the EDN main state machine can return to `Idle` without clearing those replay FIFOs.

## Expected Behavior
Disabling EDN must fully terminate the current auto request session. Once the disable transition completes and the EDN main state machine reaches `Idle`, both auto-command replay FIFOs for `GENERATE_CMD` and `RESEED_CMD` must be empty, just as they are after `CTRL.CMD_FIFO_RST`, after boot-time completion, or after leaving auto request mode by clearing `CTRL.AUTO_REQ_MODE`. No command words from the previous auto request session should remain queued after the block has been disabled.

## Actual Behavior
If EDN is disabled directly from an active auto request state, stale generate and reseed command words can remain queued even after the block returns to `Idle`. The disable path does not leave the EDN in a clean disabled state.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the EDN auto request control path, specifically the EDN main state machine and the replay FIFOs that hold automatic `generate` and `reseed` commands for CSRNG traffic.

## Trigger Condition
Program EDN for auto request mode, populate the `GENERATE_CMD` and `RESEED_CMD` replay FIFOs, and then disable EDN by clearing `CTRL.EDN_ENABLE` without first leaving auto request mode through `CTRL.AUTO_REQ_MODE`. The bug appears when the disable path forces the EDN main state machine back to `Idle` from an active auto request state.

title: [mbx] Improve Abort handling, and recovery from communications failure.
body:
This PR implements a FW-initiated reset of the Inbound and Outbound data paths in the event of a communications failure within the SoC<->mailbox<->TL-UL chain and improves the Abort handling.

_Mailbox operation is critical to all communication between the SoC and RoT, and use of the asynchronous reset of the IP block is considered infeasible because it is common to many other IP blocks._


The logic is currently reliant upon everything completing as expected (whether successfully or by an error being indicated by the TL-UL device/bus), but is not robust against potential design flaws nor against any reliability issues with the specific physical device. Further, the current Error and Abort handling mechanisms do not have the capacity to reset fully the internal state of the mailbox logic. ([Issue detailed here](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan-integrated/issues/708).)

To help with understanding this PR, the Abort mechanism is described below:

- in the event of a failure in the Request/Response mechanism, the SoC side has the capacity to request that an operation be Aborted and it is expected that this mechanism be used in response to a communications timeout (of the order of > 1 second).
- the Abort request is signaled to the RoT via an interrupt.
- the RoT firmware acknowledges the Abort condition.

It is worth noting that the SoC side itself may become stalled and unable to employ the Abort mechanism, since a Write Data access from the SoC when sending the Request may cause the SoC to be blocked upon completion of the previous write. Similarly, a Read Data access from the SoC when fetching the Response will block until the read data is retrieved from the mailbox SRAM.

It is therefore proposed that the Abort acknowledgment should be available as a RoT FW-initiated reset of the mailbox logic, for use even if there has been no explicit Abort request from the SoC side.

This PR consists of two commits:

**Commit 1:** Introduces a reset of the following internal state when the RoT FW ('host') acknowledges an Abort condition.

- u_ombx.u_req_state <- TL-UL read request
- u_ombx.u_pop_entry <- ditto
- u_ombx.u_pending <- SoC side Write Data Register stall
- u_imbx.u_req_state <- TL-UL write request
- u_imbx.u_pending <- ditto

It also clears down the count of outstanding TL-UL bus requests (`u_sramrwarb.u_outstanding_req_cnt`) and suppresses any subsequent TL-UL read response from being propagated into the Outbound mailbox logic, because that previously would result in the logic re-entering an active state as if starting to send a fresh Response to the SoC side.

**Commit 2:** Prioritizes the host-side Abort acknowledgement over all FSM states such that it may be used as a FW-initiated reset at any time, and not just when handling an explicit Abort request from the SoC. This would be used after a timeout in the communications from/to the SoC side. (Apologies: This changes the FSM identation and confuses diff tools.)

This should address [issue 708](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan-integrated/issues/708) although DV is currently unable to verify the existing Abort handling or the complete efficacy of this change. The smoke test still passes as expected.

commits.message:
[mbx] Fault recovery via Abort mechanism

Clearing of Abort condition resets both inbound and outbound
traffic, clears down the count of outstanding requests and
suppresses any subsequent core-side TL-UL read responses.
Since the Abort request clears Ready, keep the Read Data
register zeroed until the abort is acknowledged.

Signed-off-by: Adrian Lees <a.lees@lowrisc.org>

[mbx] Abort acknowledgement always resets FSMs.

Abort acknowledgement is of the highest priority, permitting
its use as a FW-driven reset mechanism even if there was no
explicit SoC-side Abort request.

Signed-off-by: Adrian Lees <a.lees@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: [hmac] Revise localparams to have unique and meaningful names
resolved_issues.body:
The issue #701 is reported by @imphil

Problem:

    Previous version of `hmac_pkg.sv` has duplicated names `k`. `k` is
    used as localparam and also used as an argument in `compress()`
    function.

The `k` in localparam is the first 32bit of fractional part for the
cubic root of the first 64 primes. So the name is changed to have the
meaning.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's mailbox (mbx) IP carries request and response traffic between the SoC and the Root of Trust (RoT). The inbound mailbox accepts request data written by the SoC, and the outbound mailbox presents response data for the SoC to read. After a communication failure or timeout on this path, RoT firmware must be able to acknowledge the abort condition and use that acknowledgement as a firmware-driven reset of the mailbox control logic, even when the SoC cannot complete the normal abort handshake first.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the mbx IP's inbound and outbound mailbox control state machines, including the outbound Ready indication during abort recovery.

## Expected Behavior
When RoT firmware acknowledges the abort condition, the mailbox must immediately return to its idle state regardless of which mailbox FSM state is currently active. This must work while the inbound mailbox is already in its write phase and while the outbound mailbox is already in its read/response phase. For an outbound transaction, the same abort acknowledgement must also clear the Ready indication for the aborted response. After that reset, the mailbox must be able to start a new inbound or outbound transaction normally.

## Actual Behavior
In the current implementation, an abort acknowledgement from RoT firmware is not honored once the mailbox FSM has already left idle. If the inbound mailbox is already accepting write data, or the outbound mailbox is already in its read/response phase, the FSM can remain in its active state instead of returning to idle. On the outbound side, Ready can also remain asserted for an aborted response. As a result, the aborted transaction is not fully cleared and the mailbox does not reliably recover for the next transaction.

## Trigger Condition
This bug is triggered when a mailbox transaction is already active and RoT firmware acknowledges the abort condition during recovery from a communication failure or timeout. It also occurs when that acknowledgement is used as a firmware-driven reset without a preceding SoC-side abort request, which is needed when the SoC is stalled and cannot complete the explicit abort sequence.

title: [keymgr_dpe, rtl] Fix key switching during erase
body:
Fixes https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan-integrated/issues/688

In comparison to https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan-integrated/pull/698, this PR handles two changes:

- If the operation is erase or disabled, do not let ctrl take over the key interface on sideload ctrl side.
- Randomize key output from keymgr_dpe_ctrl more strictly, in the sense that invalid operations present randomized keys.

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[keymgr_dpe] Fix kmac key bug on erase

The keymgr slot key is used during
advance or generate operations to drive KMAC
key interface. I.e. slot key takes precedence
over sideloaded KMAC key during advance
or generate operations (even if they are invalid).

On the other hand, the actual key value
presented by ctrl is randomized if the ongoing
advance or generate operation is invalid.

Signed-off-by: Fatih Balli <fatihballi@google.com>

resolved_issues.body: Add sections to explain how to pull PR and amend other's pending PR

fix_patch:
diff --git a/hw/ip/keymgr_dpe/rtl/keymgr_dpe_ctrl.sv b/hw/ip/keymgr_dpe/rtl/keymgr_dpe_ctrl.sv
index 2a45e6fead26e..1cc9163c502b5 100644
--- a/hw/ip/keymgr_dpe/rtl/keymgr_dpe_ctrl.sv
+++ b/hw/ip/keymgr_dpe/rtl/keymgr_dpe_ctrl.sv
@@ -210,15 +210,18 @@ module keymgr_dpe_ctrl
     end
   end
 
-  // prevents unknowns from reaching the outside world.
-  // - whatever operation causes the input data select to be disabled should not expose the key
-  //   state.
-  // - when there are no operations, the key state also should be exposed.
-  assign key_o.valid = op_req;
-
-  // Check invalidity of the slot
+  // The key released from this ctrl interface is MUXed in sideload_ctrl. The
+  // following bit decides whether the slot secret or sideload key is used to
+  // drive KMAC key interface.
+  assign key_o.valid = adv_req || gen_req;
+
+  // If requested operation is invalid or does not need the key, then pass
+  // random data to sideload ctrl interface.
+  logic release_real_key;
+  assign release_real_key = active_key_slot_o.valid && !invalid_op &&
+                            (adv_req || gen_req);
   for (genvar i = 0; i < Shares; i++) begin : gen_key_out_assign
-    assign key_o.key[i] = active_key_slot_o.valid ?
+    assign key_o.key[i] = release_real_key ?
                           active_key_slot_o.key[i] :
                           {EntropyRounds{entropy_i[i]}};
   end

problem_statement:
## Description
Key Manager DPE (DICE Protection Environment) can expose a real slot secret on the KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) sideload key interface when software starts an `erase` operation. Each DPE slot stores a secret, and only derivation operations that actively use KMAC should be allowed to present that secret to the KMAC key path. `erase` is only supposed to clear the selected slot; it must not cause the controller to switch KMAC over to the slot secret.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the `keymgr_dpe_ctrl` output path that drives the KMAC sideload key interface for the currently selected DPE slot.

## Expected Behavior
When an `erase` request is issued, the KMAC sideload output from `keymgr_dpe_ctrl` must remain invalid as a real key source, and the key data presented on that interface must stay randomized instead of exposing the selected slot secret. Only key-derivation operations such as `advance` or `generate` may present a real slot key to KMAC.

## Actual Behavior
If Key Manager DPE has already reached its normal available state and a valid slot is selected, starting an `erase` operation can make `keymgr_dpe_ctrl` drive that slot's real secret onto the KMAC sideload interface and mark it as a valid key source even though no derivation is taking place.

## Trigger Conditions
This bug is triggered when Key Manager DPE is in its normal available state with a valid active slot secret, and software issues an `erase` operation for that slot.

problem_statement:
## Description
The affected functionality is the Key Manager DPE (DICE Protection Environment) advance path that prepares input data for KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) when software derives a new DICE (Device Identifier Composition Engine) context from a source slot. A slot becomes invalid after a successful erase operation. If software later issues another advance using that erased slot as the source, the operation is reported as a failure, but the data sent on the `kmac_data_req` bus is still treated as valid advance message material.

## Expected Behavior
An advance request whose source slot has been erased must not present valid derivation data to KMAC. The advance should fail, and any KMAC input associated with that failed advance must be marked invalid so randomized data is used instead of real advance message material from the erased slot.

## Actual Behavior
After a slot is populated and then erased, a subsequent advance that reuses that slot as the source fails at the operation-status level, but the KMAC-side request still carries data marked as valid. As a result, an invalid advance on an erased slot can drive non-randomized advance message material on the KMAC input path.

## Trigger Condition
A Key Manager DPE slot is first populated by a successful advance operation, then erased, and then used again as the source of another advance request while the block is otherwise operational.

title: [rv_dm] Return blank 0x0 response when DMI side is gated
body:
This is in preparation for #20508 in order to fix the RV_DM behavior when it is gated.
Specifically, the RV_DM is supposed to return valid all-zero responses when it is not available, instead of creating a bus error that then gets translated into an error condition inside the TAP.

resolved_issues.title: [darjeeling] Add a single TAP with TL-UL as the DMI
resolved_issues.body:
Rewire JTAG to place lc_ctrl and rv_dm on the same TAP, and use dedicated DIOs for JTAG at the top. Generate a RAL model for the new TL-UL interconnect, and use it in DV. Also fix up macro names in software for the new lc_ctrl named register interfaces.

rv_dm is located at address 0 in the map. This is required by the RISC-V Debug specification, as it is the first Debug Module. If other Debug Modules are to be used, they could be placed elsewhere on the TL-UL network, and the nextdm CSR for the first DM would point to the base address of the next.

lc_ctrl is currently located at 0x20000 in the map. This may be changed to match data sheet and/or flexibility preferences. This address currently must be hard-coded (or chained to the number of DMI abits), as there is no method specified for probing this address. Only the IDCODE and what can be read from the DTMCS register are currently usable keys for finding out the DMI addresses. Alternative mechanisms are left for future discussions.

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace (+submodules)
cd /home/opentitan
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx
git checkout 5ca63ecc503427a3c7a4d6b0f8f1c78c7426a2a6
git submodule update --init --recursive

# Stage 2: install repository apt dependencies (if present)
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
if [[ -f apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing apt dependencies from apt-requirements.txt"
  cp apt-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  sed -i -e '/^$/d' -e '/^#/d' -e 's/#.*//' /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  if [[ -s /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
    apt-get update
    xargs -r apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends < /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  else
    echo "[INFO] apt-requirements.txt is empty after filtering comments"
  fi
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[WARN] apt-requirements.txt not found at 5ca63ecc503427a3c7a4d6b0f8f1c78c7426a2a6; skipping repo-specific apt install"
fi

# Stage 3: install project-specific Python dependencies from the checked-out repo
if [[ -f python-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Python deps from python-requirements.txt"
  python -m pip install -U pip "setuptools<66.0.0"
  cp python-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
  python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re

path = Path("/tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt")
lines = []
for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    stripped = line.strip()
    if stripped in {
        "types-dataclasses",
        "types-pkg_resources",
    }:
        continue
    line = re.sub(r'(#egg=[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\s+[<>=!~].*', r'\1', line)
    lines.append(line)
path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
PY
  python -m pip install -r /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt --no-warn-script-location
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[ERROR] python-requirements.txt not found at 5ca63ecc503427a3c7a4d6b0f8f1c78c7426a2a6"
  exit 1
fi

# Stage 4: install RISC-V toolchain + Verible, then persist their PATH
if [[ -f util/get-toolchain.py ]]; then
  toolchain_version=""
  if [[ -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
    toolchain_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
  fi

  echo "[INFO] Installing RISC-V toolchain via util/get-toolchain.py"
  if [[ -n "$toolchain_version" ]]; then
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update -r "$toolchain_version"
  else
    echo "[WARN] RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION not found; falling back to util/get-toolchain.py defaults"
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update
  fi
else
  echo "[WARN] util/get-toolchain.py not found at 5ca63ecc503427a3c7a4d6b0f8f1c78c7426a2a6; skipping RISC-V toolchain install"
fi

verible_version=""
if [[ -f hw/tool_requirements.py ]]; then
  verible_version="$(python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

ns = {}
exec(Path("hw/tool_requirements.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), ns)
reqs = ns.get("__TOOL_REQUIREMENTS__", {})
entry = reqs.get("verible", "")
if isinstance(entry, dict):
    print(entry.get("min_version", ""))
elif isinstance(entry, str):
    print(entry)
PY
)"
fi
if [[ -z "$verible_version" && -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
  verible_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG VERIBLE_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
fi

if [[ -n "$verible_version" ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing Verible ${verible_version}"
  rm -rf /tools/verible
  mkdir -p /tools/verible

  verible_url=""
  for candidate in \
    "https://github.com/chipsalliance/verible/releases/download/${verible_version}/verible-${verible_version}-linux-static-x86_64.tar.gz" \
    "https://github.com/chipsalliance/verible/releases/download/${verible_version}/verible-${verible_version}-Ubuntu-22.04-jammy-x86_64.tar.gz" \
    "https://github.com/chipsalliance/verible/releases/download/${verible_version}/verible-${verible_version}-Ubuntu-20.04-focal-x86_64.tar.gz"; do
    if curl -f -Ls -o /tmp/verible.tar.gz "$candidate"; then
      verible_url="$candidate"
      break
    fi
  done

  if [[ -n "$verible_url" ]]; then
    echo "[INFO] Downloaded Verible from ${verible_url}"
    tar -C /tools/verible -xf /tmp/verible.tar.gz --strip-components=1
    rm -f /tmp/verible.tar.gz
  else
    echo "[WARN] Failed to download Verible ${verible_version}; continuing without Verible"
    rm -rf /tools/verible
  fi
else
  echo "[WARN] Unable to determine Verible version from hw/tool_requirements.py or util/container/Dockerfile"
fi

cat > /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh <<'EOF'
for d in /tools/riscv/bin /tools/verible/bin; do
  [ -d "$d" ] && export PATH="$d:$PATH"
done
EOF

if ! grep -q "/etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" /etc/opentitan_bash_env; then
  echo "source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" >> /etc/opentitan_bash_env
fi
source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh

python -m pip show edalize fusesoc hjson >/dev/null
if command -v riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[INFO] RISC-V toolchain ready: $(riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc --version | head -n1)"
else
  echo "[WARN] riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc not found after Stage 4"
fi
if command -v verible-verilog-lint >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[INFO] Verible ready: $(verible-verilog-lint --version | head -n1)"
else
  echo "[WARN] verible-verilog-lint not found after Stage 4"
fi
problem_statement:
## Description
The affected block is the RISC-V Debug Module (RV_DM) DMI-facing TL-UL (TileLink Uncached Lightweight) access path that serves the debug-module register space. When access to RV_DM has been gated and the debug module is unavailable behind the DMI (Debug Module Interface) transport, a DMI read is currently turned into a TL-UL error response instead of the defined blank reply.

## Expected Behavior
If RV_DM is unavailable behind the DMI transport, a read of the RV_DM register space must still complete with a valid non-error response. The returned data must be all zeros, and the response must not indicate an access error.

## Actual Behavior
When the DMI-side path is gated, reading the RV_DM register space produces an error response rather than a valid all-zero response.

## Trigger Conditions
The bug appears when a DMI read targets the RV_DM register space while the DMI transport itself is still present, but access to RV_DM has been gated off by the debug-access controls.

title: [keymgr_dpe,rtl] Fix disabling
body:
This fixes the problems with `keymgr_dpe` disabling reported in #20468 (thereby closes that issue) and additionally prevents the wiping of sideload and SW-visible keys during disablement, which is against `keymgr_dpe`'s specification. Please see the commit messages for details.

This supersedes #20471.

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[keymgr_dpe,rtl] Remove `Quick` from `SlotQuickWipeAll`

There's no non-"quick" wiping, so let's get rid of this adjective.

Co-authored-by: Fatih Balli <fatihballi@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

[keymgr_dpe,rtl] Fix disabling (1/2)

This fixes two bugs with disabling, as reported in #20468:
- The status of the operation indefinitely remained `OpWip`.  This gets
  fixed by feeding disable requests through `keymgr_dpe_op_state_ctrl`
  and letting it drive `ack_o` (same as it does for erase requests).
- The key slots did not get cleared.  This gets fixed also by feeding
  disable requests through `keymgr_dpe_op_state_ctrl` and letting it
  drive `update_o` and by letting the Op Update Mux wipe the internal
  slots on an update from a disable request.

As `op_req` in `keymgr_dpe_ctrl` needs to be high for one cycle upon a
disable request but not during the `StCtrlDpeDisabled` state (during
which operations are illegal), this commit adds a transient state
`StCtrlDpeDisabling` that does the request.

Co-authored-by: Fatih Balli <fatihballi@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

[keymgr_dpe,rtl] Fix disabling (2/2)

Prior to this commit, `keymgr_dpe` would also wipe the sideload and
SW-visible keys on disablement.  However, our specification defines that
these must remain valid and only the internal key slots must be wiped on
disablement.  This commit fixes `keymgr_dpe` to wipe only its internal
key slots on disablement.

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: [keymgr_dpe] successful disable operation leads to OpDoneFail status
resolved_issues.body:
### desc


![image](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/assets/137649869/e02fa9c8-0603-4848-91de-9323fb303bf4)
![image](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/assets/137649869/1907ea39-7f31-4452-a98a-54dcb245a205)
![image](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/assets/137649869/1730a2d9-ca35-4015-880d-736d82a4be65)


When issuing a disable operation, it succeeds in moving the working state into disabled, however the status goes into OpDoneFail, this seems to be a result from passing into the StCtrlDpeDisabled state and immediately checking for a start condition. Typically the start register remains high until the operation is completed.  In the screenshot I gave you see that the op_start_i signal is 1, due to the operation still in progress by the time the internal state enters StCtrlDpeDisabled. 

The other issue I see is that the key_slots were not erased, this may be a result of the status of the operation ultimately failing.

resolved_issues.title: [keymgr_dpe, rtl] Fix disable request
resolved_issues.body:
#20468 reports that disable has two bugs:
1) it does not clean/erase internal keymgr slots
2) it does not correctly update status after the operation.

This commit adds an internal state to op_state_ctrl, so that disable commands also get a 1 clock cycle delayed handshake signals `op_update_o` and `op_ack_o`. These signals are used to clean keymgr slots and update the operation status.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan `keymgr_dpe` (Key Manager DPE) IP mishandles a software-triggered disable operation after the block has been initialized and a valid internal key slot exists. A disable request is legal from the `Available` working state, but the command does not complete as a successful disable sequence.

## Expected Behavior
When software programs `CONTROL_SHADOWED.OPERATION` to `Disable` and starts the command while `keymgr_dpe` is in the `Available` state, the software-visible operation status must complete as `OpDoneSuccess`, the exposed working state must become `Disabled`, and the internal key slots maintained by `keymgr_dpe` must be erased as part of entering `Disabled`.

## Actual Behavior
After a prior `Advance` operation has moved `keymgr_dpe` into `Available` and populated an internal key slot, issuing `Disable` moves the working state toward `Disabled` but does not complete as a clean successful operation. The software-visible operation status does not report successful completion for the disable command (reported observations for this bug include the status remaining `OpWip` or reaching a failure status instead of `OpDoneSuccess`), and the internal key slots are left uncleared.

## Affected Function
This affects the `keymgr_dpe` disable-command path: the control and operation-state logic that accepts a disable request in the `Available` state, reports completion status to software, and wipes internal key slots when entering `Disabled`.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when software issues a `Disable` operation from the `Available` state, especially after an `Advance` operation has created a valid internal key slot.

title: [rtl,pwrmgr] Fix escalation timeout persistence
body:
The escalation timeout needs to persist until reset. The timeout is detected by clk_i, but the timeout is used to drive a flop clocked by clk_lc. This change adds a synchronizer from clk_i to clk_lc, and a clk_lc flop reset by rst_lc_n. The output of this flop is used to set the fault_status and as a reset request.

Fixes #20516

repo.name: opentitan
repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[rtl,pwrmgr] Fix escalation timeout persistence

The escalation timeout needs to persist until reset. The timeout is detected by
clk_i, but the timeout is used to drive a flop clocked by clk_lc. This change
adds a synchronizer from clk_i to clk_lc, and a clk_lc flop reset by rst_lc_n.
The output of this flop is used to set the fault_status and as a reset request.

With this fix the pwrmgr_escalation_reset test passes at the block level.

Fixes #20516

Signed-off-by: Guillermo Maturana <maturana@opentitan.org>

resolved_issues.title: [rtl,pwrmgr] escalation timeout should persist
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

If the escalation network stops for more than 128 cycles, pwrmgr should request an escalation reset, per https://opentitan.org/book/hw/top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/pwrmgr/doc/theory_of_operation.html#escalation-clock-timeout.

However, the escalation timeout condition (esc_timeout in pwrmgr.sv) does not persist, unlike esc_rst_req_d/q. This means if the escalation clock restarts soon after 128 cycles of being inactive an escalation reset won't be generated.

One simple fix would be to flop esc_timeout, similar to how esc_rst_req_d is treated.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's Power Manager (pwrmgr) contains escalation clock-timeout logic that is supposed to detect when the alert escalation path stops responding while the system is in its normal active state. If the escalation clock remains inactive for more than 128 pwrmgr clock cycles, pwrmgr must treat that as an escalation fault and initiate a local escalation reset.

## Expected Behavior
A stall shorter than the 128-cycle timeout threshold must not trigger an escalation reset. Once the escalation clock has been inactive long enough to exceed that threshold, the timeout condition must persist until reset handling takes effect. Even if the escalation clock starts toggling again shortly after the threshold is crossed, pwrmgr must still disable CPU fetch and issue the escalation reset request.

## Actual Behavior
The timeout condition is not persistent. If the escalation clock stops for only slightly more than the timeout threshold and then restarts soon afterward, pwrmgr can lose the fault indication before the reset path reacts to it. In that case, CPU fetch remains enabled and no escalation reset request is generated even though the timeout threshold was exceeded.

## Trigger Condition
This bug is triggered in the pwrmgr escalation timeout path when the escalation clock is halted just over the 128-cycle limit and then restarted before the fault has been latched as a persistent reset condition. Very long stalls still trigger the reset reliably, so the failure is most visible in near-threshold cases.

title: [spi_device] Fix up synchronization of status bits
body:
This PR builds on top of #21119 . Only the last two commits are new.

### Enable continuously polled status registers

Previously, the Read Status Register commands behaved differently from
the SPI flash convention, holding a fixed value for every word clocked
out of the same command + rotating through all three registers for each
command. Change the commands to only return the byte targeted by the
specific command, and update the status register value at every byte
beat (8th posedge of SCK).

This brings the SPI device flash behavior in line with the convention,
which is to allow hosts to poll the same register repeatedly and see
updated values as it goes along.

Disable the scoreboard's validation of Read Status commands for now. It
uses csr_rd() to determine the resolved value, but this is impossible.
The source of truth is in the SPI domain, and it updates at a much more
frequent interval than the core clock domain: The SPI domain updates for
every 8th posedge of SCK, whereas the core clock domain's view updates
only at every CSB de-assertion (delayed by synchronization to an async
domain).

In addition, add a CSR to permit resetting the async FIFO used to bring
software-originated status register changes into the SPI clock domain.

### Write mode and status bits alongside the command
Write some pertinent mode and status bits to the cmdfifo alongside the
command. The BUSY and WEL bits can be used to determine whether an
uploaded command should be accepted, and the address mode bit helps
determine whether an associated address in the addrfifo should be
interpreted as 3 bytes or 4 bytes.

Uploading these bits alongside the command byte avoids race conditions
with software checking their values after the transaction actually
occurs.

Make WEL an explicit field in the FLASH_STATUS CSR, and mark it as only
RW0C. Like the BUSY bit, software has no need to set this field to 1. It
should only clear it when it completes uploaded commands. Making it RW0C
eliminates the need for read-modify-write cycles just for checking
hardware-writable bits.

### Related issues
https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/16411 is related, but this doesn't do enough to handle it. We would need to know if the address phase was cut short.

Resolves #20754

resolved_issues.title: [spi_device] Synchronize control and status bits at regular intervals
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

spi_device still does not handle status bits like a host would expect of a SPI flash device. The commit phase of status bit synchronization currently only occurs on the rising edge of CSB, but the ReadStatus commands need to allow for changes to the WIP bit _without_ the deassertion of CSB.

This design confuses the visibility of status bits with the requirements for the passthrough gate. It is only the passthrough gate that must wait for the deassertion of CSB to switch on/off.

Instead, for the purposes of representing the status registers, commit staged bits at every 8th SCK edge. Keep the current staging mechanism for synchronization, and also keep the passthrough gate commit on CSB de-assertion.

Semi-related, in that it could use a similar commit point: https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/15543

resolved_issues.title: [spi_device] Incoming address size cannot be validated
resolved_issues.body:
In flash/passthrough modes, the spi_device IP does not give any indication of how long the transaction actually was, so transactions using the wrong address mode may pass through. This might only be of interest for invalidating shortened Sector Erase transactions, where 3 bytes of address was provided when the address mode required 4 bytes of address.

This is tagged for a future release. It falls into the category of robustness in an environment with errors, but it is not critical for the current stepping.

[Effort estimate](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/16411#issuecomment-1481325048_) by @hcallahan-lowrisc: 
> I'm not super confident on this estimate and hence I have leaned towards pessimism. If it is not deferred, recommend to re-evaluate.
>
> estimate 16
> remaining 2023-03-23 16

resolved_issues.title: [spi_device] Fix address mode synchronization
resolved_issues.body:
### Relax stringent CSB pulse width requirements:
Add a new edge-to-toggle synchronizer + filter module for SPI to remove
the stringent CSB pulse width requirements that fell out of using
prim_edge_detector to detect CSB de-assertion.

spid_csb_sync produces a pulse in the sys_clk domain when a CSB-clocked
flop produces a value change, compared against the last seen value in
the sys_clk domain. The toggling flop input signal gets filtered based
on (1) whether any SPI clocks were observed and (2) whether the
toggle_en_i signal was asserted for one of those SPI clocks.

In addition to merely providing the notification that a transaction has
completed, this module is also used in the spid_upload module for
qualifying whether an uploaded command was written (for the interrupt
event).

### Harmonize address mode syncs to byte beats
Simplify address mode synchronization by using a common commit point at
the end of the command phase. Add a sync pulse for the address mode to
commit at the 8th posedge of the SPI clock. This allows enough time for
software-originated changes to cross into the SPI domain and be picked
up for the next command. In addition, there is no need to reset the
entire spi_device IP when changing address modes after a period of SPI
activity.

Harmonize address calculations to align with this commit point. The
passthrough and upload modules have slightly different mechanisms, but
they now use the address mode from this point. The passthrough module
uses the registered value, but the upload module uses the D side of that
flop instead. The upload module may need this information for some
future enhancements related to metadata committed to the command FIFO.

In addition, inform software when a software-originated address mode
change is still pending. This may occur if no transactions occurred
since the last software write. When a write is pending, the value shown
is the pending value, not the current committed one in hardware.
However, that pending value will be picked up in time for the next
command. If the desired value is different from the prior write,
software may overwrite, as long as the SPI host is known to be inactive.

### Related issues
Fixes #15543, https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/15721

--- a/hw/ip/spi_device/doc/theory_of_operation.md
+++ b/hw/ip/spi_device/doc/theory_of_operation.md
@@ -81,9 +81,11 @@ It means the update happens when the next SPI transaction is received.
 The BUSY bit in the CSR is the synchronized value of the STATUS BUSY bit in the SPI clock domain.
 Due to the CDC latency, SW may see the updated value (BUSY clear) with long delay.
 
-WEL bit can be controlled by SW and also by HW.
+The WEL bit can get updates from both HW and SW.
 HW updates WEL bit when it receives WREN(06h) or WRDI(04h) commands.
 The opcode can be configured via [`CMD_INFO_WREN`](registers.md#cmd_info_wren) and [`CMD_INFO_WRDI`](registers.md#cmd_info_wrdi).
+Meanwhile, SW may clear the WEL bit when it completes the received commands.
+Note that SW may only clear the WEL bit.
 
 The SW update of the STATUS register via [`FLASH_STATUS`](registers.md#flash_status) is not instantaneous.
 The IP stores the SW request into the asynchronous FIFO then the request is processed in the SPI clock domain.
@@ -93,6 +95,14 @@ SW sees the committed registers when reading the [`FLASH_STATUS`](registers.md#f
 
 The attached host system also reads back the committed registers via Read Status commands.
 This scheme is to guarantee the atomicity of the STATUS register.
+On every 8th SPI clock cycle, the SPI domain commits the latest resolved value to the committed registers.
+Each byte beat of the Read Status commands will return the latest committed value of the targeted register.
+A Read Status commands can thus repeatedly poll the BUSY bit and see updates in the same transaction.
+
+Again, note that the passthrough gate only updates after CSB makes a 0->1 transition, and it derives its value from the committed BUSY bit.
+After the BUSY bit is set, there must be at least one command before the gate will open again.
+Typically, a Read Status command follows any command that would set the BUSY bit, to check that the BUSY bit has cleared.
+This activity is sufficient to unblock passthrough for the next command.
 
 If the host sends the Write Status commands, the commands are not processed in this module.
 SW must configure the remaining command information entries to upload the Write Status commands to the FIFOs.
@@ -213,10 +223,14 @@ The `addr_mode` is used to determine the address size in the command.

+Included are the state of the address mode, the BUSY status bit, and the WEL status bit at the time the command was uploaded.

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan SPI Device IP, when configured in flash mode to emulate an SPI flash device, does not return Read Status Register data the way an SPI flash host expects during a single transaction. After a Read Status Register command selects one of the status-register bytes, the response stream can advance to other status-register bytes on later byte beats instead of continuing to return the byte selected by that command.

## Expected Behavior
While chip select bar (CSB) remains asserted for one Read Status Register transaction, the SPI Device must keep returning the same status-register byte targeted by that command on every byte clocked out in that transaction. This must hold for continuous polling of status register byte 0, byte 1, or byte 2: each command should repeatedly return only its own selected byte until CSB is deasserted.

## Actual Behavior
Instead, when a host keeps CSB asserted and clocks out multiple bytes after issuing a Read Status Register command, the SPI Device can rotate across the three status-register bytes. As a result, continuous polling of one status-register byte within a single transaction may return data from other status-register byte positions.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the SPI Device IP flash-mode status register read-response path, specifically the SPI-clock-domain logic that selects which status-register byte is returned for Read Status Register commands.

## Trigger Condition
The bug is triggered when the SPI Device IP is in flash mode and an upstream SPI host performs continuous polling by keeping CSB asserted while clocking out multiple bytes from a single Read Status Register transaction.

problem_statement:
## Description
The UART IP is intended to treat FIFO watermark interrupts as level-sensitive status conditions rather than edge-triggered events. In the failing behavior here, the transmit FIFO watermark interrupt (`tx_watermark`) still acts like an event interrupt, so the interrupt state and interrupt output do not reliably reflect the live TX FIFO watermark condition.

## Expected Behavior
`tx_watermark` should continuously reflect whether the transmit FIFO depth is below the configured transmit watermark threshold. If the TX FIFO starts empty or is cleared, `tx_watermark` should already be asserted. If software writes to clear interrupt state while the TX FIFO remains below the threshold, `tx_watermark` should stay asserted. The interrupt should deassert only after the TX FIFO depth moves back to the non-watermark side of the threshold. `tx_empty` is a separate interrupt and is not the behavior being changed here.

## Actual Behavior
`tx_watermark` behaves like a one-shot or edge/event interrupt. It can be deasserted even while the TX FIFO is still below the configured watermark threshold, and it may only assert again after another threshold crossing occurs.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the UART IP's interrupt generation and interrupt-state reporting for the transmit FIFO watermark condition (`tx_watermark`).

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears when UART watermark interrupts are enabled and the TX FIFO is below the configured watermark threshold without a fresh crossing event, especially immediately after the TX FIFO is cleared or after transmission drains the FIFO back below the threshold.

title: [kmac] Change fifo_empty interrupt type to status
body:
This resolves #21049.

~~Note that this PR currently contains a cherry-picked commit from @msfschaffner . In addition, some automated TLT sequence needs to be adjusted as well for this PR to pass CI. I am mainly creating now for the sake of visilbility.~~
Together with @andreaskurth , I've come to the conclusion that it is better to not signal the empty status interrupt if software is not using the module. For example, software shouldn't get interrupted if an application interface is using KMAC (the app interface will handle the FIFO condition autonomously) or if the KMAC block is completely idle. But only if the FIFO runs empty while software is using the block and had to stop writing data at some point. I've now changed the design accordingly. This should work independently of potential TLT changes and CIP library modifications.
 
Since this change is software visible, one could argue to create a new version of the IP for this which would also require to go back to D1/V1. However, it seems that the current software only uses the untouched `Done` and `Err` interrupts but not the `FIFO_Empty` interrupt changed with this PR. For example:
- Grepping for `KMAC_INTR_ENABLE_FIFO_EMPTY`, i.e. the bit offset for enabling the interrupt in software yields nothing.
- Grepping for `KMAC_INTR_STATE_FIFO_EMPTY` gives one hit inside `sw/device/silicon_creator/lib/drivers/kmac_unittest.cc` only.
- Grepping for `KMAC_INTR_TEST_FIFO_EMPTY` just gives the SV parameter definition for the reset value of this bit in `kmac_reg_pkg.sv` (auto-generated).
- Grepping for `KMAC_INTR_COMMON_FIFO_EMPTY` gives one function `kmac_get_irq_bit_index()` inside `sw/device/lib/dif/autogen/dif_kmac_autogen.c`. This function is called from within
  - `dif_kmac_irq_is_pending()`
  - `dif_kmac_irq_acknowledge()`
  - `dif_kmac_irq_force()`
  - `dif_kmac_irq_set_enabled()`
  - `dif_kmac_irq_set_enabled()`
  None of these functions are called with `kDifKmacIrqFifoEmpty` as argument.

Most likely, FIFO empty interrupt is not used because it's not very usable as long as it's of type "event". I thus suggest avoid the hassle and not introduce a new version and remain at D2S/V2S if possible.

commits.message:
[kmac] Rework fifo_empty interrupt, change type to status

The type of this interrupt is changed from event to status. To make the
interrupt more usable for software, it only fires if the message FIFO
has run full previously (e.g., if the SHA3 core is currently busy
or if the KMAC block is waiting for entropy from EDN). Under normal
circumstances, the hardware empties the FIFO much faster than software
filling it, so there is no point in interrupting software to tell it
to run faster.

Also, the interrupt can now only fire if software can actually write
the message FIFO.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#21049.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

### Description

KMAC-specific issue of https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/15378

KMAC has the following interrupts:
- kmac_done : signals when the absorption has completed, event seems fine for this.
- kmac_err: signals when an error has occured, event seems fine for this.
- fifo_empty: indicates if the message FIFO is empty, status seems more sensible for this one.

+KMAC/SHA3 error occurred. ERR_CODE register shows the details
+
+### INTR_STATE . fifo_empty
+The message FIFO is empty.
+This interrupt is raised only if the message FIFO is actually writable by software, i.e., if all of the following conditions are met:
+i) The KMAC block is not exercised by a hardware application interface.
+ii) The SHA3 block is in the Absorb state.
+iii) Software has not yet written the Process command to finish the absorption process.
+For the interrupt to be raised, the message FIFO must also have been full previously.
+Otherwise, the hardware empties the FIFO faster than software can fill it and there is no point in interrupting the software to inform it about the message FIFO being empty.

+KMAC/SHA3 absorbing has been completed

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Stage 1: checkout base_sha in a clean workspace (+submodules)
cd /home/opentitan
git reset --hard
git clean -fdx
git checkout 8f1e7d92fd9984e3f335291f2cdd90c280a3b21d
git submodule update --init --recursive

# Stage 2: install repository apt dependencies (if present)
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
if [[ -f apt-requirements.txt ]]; then
  echo "[INFO] Installing apt dependencies from apt-requirements.txt"

  sed -i -e '/^$/d' -e '/^#/d' -e 's/#.*//' /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt
  if [[ -s /tmp/opentitan-apt-requirements.txt ]]; then

fi

# Stage 3: install project-specific Python dependencies from the checked-out repo
if [[ -f python-requirements.txt ]]; then

  python -m pip install -U pip "setuptools<66.0.0"
  cp python-requirements.txt /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
  python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re

path = Path("/tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt")
lines = []
for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    stripped = line.strip()
    if stripped in {
        "types-dataclasses",
        "types-pkg_resources",
    }:
        continue
    line = re.sub(r'(#egg=[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)\s+[<>=!~].*', r'\1', line)
    lines.append(line)
path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
PY
  python -m pip install -r /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt --no-warn-script-location
  rm -f /tmp/opentitan-python-requirements.txt
else
  echo "[ERROR] python-requirements.txt not found at baseline"
  exit 1
fi

# Stage 4: install the RISC-V toolchain and persist PATH.
# Verible is intentionally skipped here because the derived release URL for this
# baseline currently fails during image build, while the KMAC DV flow exercised
# by tb_script relies on dvsim/FuseSoC/VCS rather than Verible.
if [[ -f util/get-toolchain.py ]]; then
  toolchain_version=""
  if [[ -f util/container/Dockerfile ]]; then
    toolchain_version="$(sed -n 's/^ARG RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION=//p' util/container/Dockerfile | head -n1)"
  fi

  echo "[INFO] Installing RISC-V toolchain via util/get-toolchain.py"
  if [[ -n "$toolchain_version" ]]; then
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update -r "$toolchain_version"
  else
    echo "[WARN] RISCV_TOOLCHAIN_TAR_VERSION not found; falling back to util/get-toolchain.py defaults"
    python util/get-toolchain.py --update
  fi
else
  echo "[WARN] util/get-toolchain.py not found at baseline; skipping RISC-V toolchain install"
fi

cat > /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh <<'EOF'
for d in /tools/riscv/bin /tools/verible/bin; do
  [ -d "$d" ] && export PATH="$d:$PATH"
done
true
EOF

if ! grep -q "/etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" /etc/opentitan_bash_env; then
  echo "source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh" >> /etc/opentitan_bash_env
fi
source /etc/opentitan_tools_path.sh

if ! python -m pip show edalize fusesoc hjson >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[WARN] One or more Python DV dependencies are not visible via pip show"
fi
if command -v riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[INFO] RISC-V toolchain ready: $(riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc --version | head -n1)"
else
  echo "[WARN] riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc not found after Stage 4"

if command -v verible-verilog-lint >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[INFO] Verible ready: $(verible-verilog-lint --version | head -n1)"
else
  echo "[WARN] verible-verilog-lint not found after Stage 4"
fi
problem_statement:
## Description
The affected functionality is the KMAC (Keccak Message Authentication Code) IP's `fifo_empty` interrupt and its software-visible `INTR_STATE.fifo_empty` bit. This interrupt reports the empty state of the message FIFO that software uses to feed data into the SHA3 absorb phase.

## Expected Behavior
`fifo_empty` should behave as a status interrupt rather than a one-shot event. `INTR_STATE.fifo_empty` must reflect the current interrupt source level. If the FIFO-empty source is still active, or if the interrupt is still being forced through `INTR_TEST.fifo_empty`, software writes that would acknowledge or clear an event interrupt must not make `INTR_STATE.fifo_empty` drop to 0. The bit should deassert only after the active source is removed.

## Actual Behavior
The design treats `fifo_empty` like an event interrupt. `INTR_STATE.fifo_empty` is latched and can be cleared by software even while the FIFO-empty status or forced interrupt condition remains active, so the register no longer reflects the live hardware state.

## Trigger Condition
The bug appears whenever software relies on `fifo_empty` as a live status signal. A concrete trigger is to force `fifo_empty` through `INTR_TEST`, observe `INTR_STATE.fifo_empty` assert, and then write `INTR_STATE.fifo_empty` to clear it: the bit incorrectly clears even though the source is still asserted.

title: [i2c,rtl] Remove double-counted t_f
body:
As titled, basically.

This change caused a lot of breakage in the i2c block level DV, which I have not been able to fully mitigate.
This is primarily around breaking the START/RSTART detection routines in the monitor, which causes the monitor to lose it's lock 
on the bus traffic.
For now, I have weakened the monitor checks for the correct Setup/Holds around these events, which mostly fixes the breakage.
There is still one test that fails systematically with this change, `i2c_host_rx_oversample`.
(On a related note, this test seems to be misnamed, as the testplan description doesn't gel with its implementation IMO. It could be a candidate for removal)

I proposed merging this RTL change with the DV mitigations for now, and removing the broken test from the regression for now. Then to create an action item to come back and fix it properly later.

Closes #18958
Goes towards #18492

https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/7545bb6eac5207c29c5413fa596b9e219403f200/hw/ip/i2c/rtl/i2c_fsm.sv#L161-L162

problem_statement:
## Description
The OpenTitan I2C IP has a host-mode timing bug in the logic that generates the I2C serial clock (SCL). When the I2C controller is acting as the bus host and software programs the host timing registers, the programmed fall-time parameter (`t_f`) is counted twice while forming each host clock pulse. This makes the SCL period observed on the bus longer than the period implied by the programmed timing values and contributes to the reported clock-speed mismatch.

## Expected Behavior
When the OpenTitan I2C controller operates in host mode, the SCL waveform seen on the bus should match the timing encoded in the programmed host timing registers, aside from normal clock-quantization effects. In particular, changing the programmed fall-time parameter (`t_f`) by N input-clock cycles should change the end-to-end SCL period by N cycles, not by 2N. The host timing logic should therefore account for `t_f` only once when deriving each host clock pulse.

## Actual Behavior
The host-side finite-state machine (FSM) adds an extra `t_f` contribution while generating the SCL pulse. As a result, host transfers with a non-zero programmed fall time produce an SCL clock that is slower than expected, and measurements of the SCL period or frequency on the bus do not match the programmed timing values.

## Affected Function
The affected logic is the OpenTitan I2C IP's host-mode SCL timing generation, specifically the FSM path that derives host clock timing from the programmed rise time (`t_r`), fall time (`t_f`), high time (`thigh`), and low time (`tlow`) parameters.

## Trigger Condition
This occurs when the I2C block is operating in host mode and generating SCL from programmed timing registers with a non-zero fall-time value. The mismatch is visible during host-driven bus transactions when the observed SCL period on the pins is compared against the programmed timing configuration.

title: [entropy_src, sha3] Fix CS AES Halt interface and entropy_src_rng_max_rate test
body:
This PR contains a couple of commits to fix the configuration of the `entropy_src_rng_max_rate` test (commits 1 and 2) and the known-to-be-broken CS AES halt interface intended to prevent power spikes at the chip level by only letting either the AES core inside CSRNG or the SHA3 core inside the entropy source run, but not both together (commits 3 and 4).

The `entropy_src_rng_max_rate` test is important to analyze the back pressure behavior of the pipeline and the CS AES halt interface (if properly working) is the main source of back pressure inside the hardware pipeline of ENTROPY_SRC.

All this is related to #21686 and #20953.

repo.description: OpenTitan: Open source silicon root of trust

commits.message:
[entropy_src/dv] Fix CS AES Halt agent configuration

A visual inspection of the CSRNG block reveales that the maximum latency
for getting a ACK on the CS AES Halt interface is actually 48 clock
cycles (the Update command takes 3 AES-256 blocks).

In addition, the agent was missing the `zero_delays = 0` configuration
parameter. As a result, any min/max delay parameters were ignored and
the agent always ACKed after a single clock cycle.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

[entropy_src/dv] Fix usage of rng_max_delay plusarg

Previously, upon reading the plusarg, the specified value was
immediately written to the configuration object of the RNG agent in the
environment config. But as it turns out, the entropy_src_env_cfg holding
the RNG agent which got the plusarg value is created before
entropy_src_env. During the creation of the latter, a new RNG agent
object is generated. This means the plusarg value got previously
overwritten.

This commit solves this issue by storing the plusarg value into a new
configuration variable that can be used in entropy_src_env to configure
the newly created RNG agent.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

[kmac, sha3] Add REQ/ACK interface to delay Keccak operations

This interface is required to be able to properly delay operations of
the SHA3-based conditioner inside the ENTROPY_SRC block until CSRNG
confirms its internal AES core is halted.

Previously, it has been tried to handle this as part of the main FSM
of ENTROPY_SRC outside of the SHA3 core. However, this is not sufficient
as in the case of ENTROPY_SRC, most SHA3 operations are actually
triggered by the sha3pad instance inside the SHA3 core.

This is related to lowRISC/OpenTitan#17941.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

[entropy_src] Fix CS AES Halt interface

Now that the SHA3 core features an interface to directly implement the
functionality to correctly sync with the AES core inside CSRNG in order
to avoid both of them becoming active at the same time, most of the
custom logic for this feature inside ENTROPY_SRC can be removed.

This resolves lowRISC/OpenTitan#17941.

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

[entropy_src] Fix a Verilator lint warning

Signed-off-by: Pirmin Vogel <vogelpi@lowrisc.org>

resolved_issues.title: [entropy_src] Make sure unaltered raw data can be extracted for FIPS randomness validation
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

Our current understanding is that no health tests will alter the data that is accumulated in the observe FIFO. FIPS validation testing, we can use the Firmware Override / Bypass Mode to read it (see [Programmer's Guide - OpenTitan Documentation](https://opentitan.org/book/hw/ip/entropy_src/doc/programmers_guide.html#firmware-override--bypass-modes)). An interrupt is generated on reaching a predefined threshold in the FIFO.

Issue created after discussion b/w: @moidx @johannheyszl VadimS @vogelpi @zi-v @h-filali

resolved_issues.title: [entropy_src] SHA3 core / Keccak active without CS AES Halt
resolved_issues.body:
`entropy_src` sometimes activates its SHA3 core (and in particular the Keccak round) without requesting CSRNG's AES to halt, as described in [this comment on issue #14193](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/14193#issuecomment-1497734855). This is against the intention of the `cs_aes_halt` interface (see the definition added in #17943). How frequently this happens varies strongly with enabling/disabling, configuration and operation mode, and entropy availability and demand.

Here's an example (`util/dvsim/dvsim.py hw/ip/entropy_src/dv/entropy_src_sim_cfg.hjson -t xcelium -r 1 -w shm -i entropy_src_rng_with_xht_rsps -s 307146402` at 86d6bcef3dcd7a589eb08c72f036ff3540e44bed):
![2023-04-12T12:09:43+00:00](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3583291/231452713-39371472-c113-43cc-8d9d-262cf9ed439b.png)
The bottom signal shows when Keccak is active and the signal just above shows when CS AES Halt is active. Clearly, Keccak is frequently active when CS AES Halt is not. The other signals show parts of the operation mode and state of `entropy_src`.

This happens in all modes: during startup, in firmware entropy insertion mode, and in FIPS mode during continuous health tests.
- When Keccak gets triggered, it runs 24 rounds, which together take 24 clock cycles (unmasked implementation).
- In firmware entropy insertion mode, I've seen as little as 200 clock cycles between two Keccak rounds. The actual lower bound may be even less, depending on SW.
- Outside firmware entropy insertion mode, there seem to be at least 512 clock cycles between two Keccak rounds.

In the short term (for M2.5), we are adding the current behavior to the specification together with assertions to ensure the implementation matches our understanding: #17943.

In the longer term, we have to decide (a) if the CS AES Halt interface is necessary at all and (b) if the current implementation is sufficient. Depending on this, we should then:
| (a) | (b) | action           |
|-----|-----|:------------------|
| no  | X   | remove interface |
| yes | no  | fix implementation    |
| yes | yes | keep status quo  |

resolved_issues.title: [entropy_src] Determine when and what FIFOs can drop entropy
resolved_issues.body:
### Description

Currently several FIFOs drop entropy on certain occasions e.g. the postht FIFO, the precon FIFO and the bypass FIFO.
We need to evaluate for each FIFO when and in what configuration it is allowed to drop data.
For the instances where FIFOs are not allowed to drop data we need to add alerts to notify the firmware that entropy has been dropped. We should also determine whether those alerts should be fatal or not. There are already fatal alerts for the esrng FIFO, the observe FIFO and the esfinal FIFO in place. However, the observe FIFO is the only one of those three that has a write error. The other two only have a read and a state error.

To determine whether there are writes to full FIFOs I wrote assertions which trigger when the FIFOs are full and they are written to.
I was able to find writes when full for the postht FIFO, the bypass FIFO and the precon FIFO. I did this both before and after [this](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/pull/21685/commits/d23d43ea543f6b83d27e7487eb0c4a5edf5bd82a) commit. For both before and after the commit I get the same result.

problem_statement:
## Description
OpenTitan's Entropy Source IP contains a SHA3/Keccak-based conditioner and a `cs_aes_halt` request/acknowledge interface to CSRNG (Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generator). This interface is intended to prevent simultaneous activity in the Entropy Source conditioner and CSRNG's internal AES engine, which can otherwise create chip-level power spikes.

## Affected Function
The affected functionality is the Entropy Source conditioner path that starts Keccak processing and coordinates that processing with CSRNG through the `cs_aes_halt` interface.

## Expected Behavior
Whenever the Entropy Source is about to start a Keccak operation, it must assert `cs_aes_halt_req`, wait until CSRNG acknowledges that its AES engine is halted, and keep the request asserted until the Keccak operation completes. Keccak must not be active in any cycle where the `cs_aes_halt` request/acknowledge handshake is not active.

## Actual Behavior
`entropy_src` can activate its SHA3/Keccak conditioner before the `cs_aes_halt` handshake is active, or while the halt request is not asserted at all. As a result, Keccak can run concurrently with CSRNG's AES engine instead of being serialized behind the halt handshake.

## Trigger Conditions
The bug is exposed when the Entropy Source is actively conditioning entropy at a sustained high rate and the conditioning pipeline experiences significant backpressure, causing Keccak operations to be triggered frequently or with very little spacing between runs.

title: [i2c] Increase depth of ACQ FIFO to 268 bytes
body:
This change allows the I2C HW IP module to absorb a max-length SMBus Block Write,
which consists of 1 command code byte, 1 byte defining the number of data bytes in the
block write, up to 255 data bytes, and 1 optional Packet Error Code
(PEC) byte; thus up to 258 bytes in total (from SMBus Specification
version 3.2, section 6.5.7).  Our I2C HW IP module additionally puts the
byte after the Start condition (which contains the address and the R/Wn
bit) and a byte for the Stop condition into the FIFO; thus the total
increases to 260 bytes.

To account for any oversights we may have made in the analysis of the
protocol, we add an extra 8 bytes as margin, thus 268 bytes.

Note that this is larger than required by MCTP, which would be 75 bytes:
- "The size of a transmission unit is defined as the size of the packet
  payload that is carried in an MCTP packet.  The [...] minimum
  transmission unit size for MCTP is 64 bytes.  A message terminus that
  supports MCTP control messages shall always accept valid packets that
  have a transmission unit equal to or less than the baseline
  transmission unit." (from MCTP Base Specification version 1.3.0,
  section 8.3)
- MCTP packets have a 4 byte header followed by the packet payload and
  they are encapsulated between a header and a tailer that is specific
  to the physical medium (from MCTP Base Specification version 1.3.0,
  section 8.1).  For MCTP on SMBus, header and tailer consist of 4 and 1
  byte, respectively (see above).
- Thus 4 + 4 + 64 + 1 = 73 bytes plus two bytes for Start and Stop
  (based on our HW IP module; see above) gives 75 bytes.

If the ACQ FIFO cannot absorb a full SMBus Block Write or MCTP control
message, real-time constraints to process bytes from the ACQ FIFO are
imposed on SW controlling the I2C HW module.  The maximum allowed delays
depend on the protocol:
- SMBus allows target devices to stretch the clock by up to 25 ms per
  message (t_LOW:CEXT in Table 14, 15, and 16 of the SMBus Specification
  version 3.2).
- MCTP allows target devices to stretch the clock by at most 250 us per
  byte (from MCTP SMBbus/I2C Transport Binding Specification version
  1.2.0, section 6.18).

In order to not impose such real-time constraints on SW for top-level
designs that use I2C with SMBus or MCTP, this commit makes the ACQ FIFO
sufficiently deep that any max-length transaction can be absorbed.  If
SW doesn't drain the ACQ FIFO once it's full before the next message,
that message should get NACK'd and the controller has to retry later --
but protocol compliance holds and the I2C lines are not blocked.
Currently our I2C HW IP module doesn't implement this NACKing, but this
will be resolved in a separate commit (see the PR of this commit for
details and links).

Block-level tests pass, except for the known failures listed in #21755, thus not caused by this PR.

commits.message:
[i2c/rtl] Remove `FifoDepth` parameter from `i2c_core`

The `FifoDepth` parameter is defined in `i2c.hjson` and its value is
reflected in the autogenerated `i2c_reg_pkg`.  Prior to this commit,
`i2c_core` defined `FifoDepth` in its parameter list and the value
defined *there* got used in RTL.  This problem did not have consequences
because the value assigned in `i2c_core` was the same as in `i2c.hjson`.
This commit fixes the problem by importing `FifoDepth` from
`i2c_reg_pkg`.

parameter into a separate, new parameter named `AcqFifoDepth`.  This
allows instantiators making the ACQ FIFO of all `i2c` instances deeper
or shallower than the other FIFOs.

For now, the new parameter is set to 64, which is equal to the value of
the `FifoDepth` parameter.

  they are encapsulated between a header and a tailer that is specific
  to the physical medium (from MCTP Base Specification version 1.3.0,
  section 8.1).  For MCTP on SMBus, header and tailer consist of 4 and 1
  byte, respectively (see above).
- Thus 4 + 4 + 64 + 1 = 73 bytes plus two bytes for Start and Stop
  (based on our HW IP module; see above) gives 75 bytes.

If the ACQ FIFO cannot absorb a full SMBus Block Write or MCTP control
message, real-time constraints to process bytes from the ACQ FIFO are
imposed on SW controlling the I2C HW module.  The maximum allowed delays
depend on the protocol:
- SMBus allows target devices to stretch the clock by up to 25 ms per
  message (t_LOW:CEXT in Table 14, 15, and 16 of the SMBus Specification
  version 3.2).
- MCTP allows target devices to stretch the clock by at most 250 us per
  byte (from MCTP SMBbus/I2C Transport Binding Specification version
  1.2.0, section 6.18).

In order to not impose such real-time constraints on SW for top-level
designs that use I2C with SMBus or MCTP, this commit makes the ACQ FIFO
sufficiently deep that any max-length transaction can be absorbed.  If
SW doesn't drain the ACQ FIFO once it's full before the next message,
that message should get NACK'd and the controller has to retry later --
but protocol compliance holds and the I2C lines are not blocked.
Currently our I2C HW IP module doesn't implement this NACKing, but this
will be resolved in a separate commit (see the PR of this commit for
details and links).

Signed-off-by: Andreas Kurth <adk@lowrisc.org>
